Opening summary: world's fever rapidly worsening as conference enters day 2

Oliver Milman

Good morning from Turkey and welcome to the second day of Cop31, the UN gathering that is taking place, again, to help prod indolent countries clear of catastrophic planetary heating.

A lot of angst was vented on the first day of the summit over whether this goal is being achieved, and even if Cop is the best forum in which to achieve it. Perhaps sensing the fractured, distracted geopolitical mood, Chris Bowen, Australia’s climate minister and Cop negotiations chief, plaintively urged countries to “show the world that multilateralism works. Let’s show the world we are equal to the challenge.”

Further evidence, if it was needed, was unveiled yesterday showing the world is failing rather badly in this challenge to stem its growing fever. But research published this morning shows carbon emissions from fossil fuels are falling slightly, and there is still hope here in Antalya that things can change. If not then, well, what are we all doing here? Right?

About 100,000 delegates crammed into the well-tended conference venue yesterday and the long queues for registration badges led the UN to plead for people to return for them today if attendance on Monday wasn’t compulsory.

Tuesday will lay the groundwork for the arrival tomorrow of leaders from more than 90 countries, with notable absentees including the heads of the US and China. Today’s theme is “energy and transport, touching on a key goal of this Cop to get the world to agree to greatly increase the share of energy used via electricity”. That power will, hopefully, be clean.

Let’s see how close to consensus the world will be on that. At the very least, the Turkish baked goods promise to be delicious and there is some tasteful art constructed of discarded waste to look at. Onwards.

As Turkey convenes world leaders to forge agreements that stop climate breakdown, its own leader is celebrating new fossil fuel exploration.

President Recep Tayyip Erdoğan, who is expected at Cop31 in Antalya later today, announced the “encouraging” discovery of two new oilfields in the Gabar mountains in a post on X last night.

“We have discovered oil in two further fields in the region. Production began in October at the fields we have named Gaziler and Çardaklı. According to our initial assessments, these two new fields hold an in-situ oil potential of 135 million barrels.”

The new fields and further wells should increase oil production by 30% in the Gabar region, which has “virtually become the capital of oil”, Erdoğan said in separate comments made after a cabinet meeting yesterday.

Burning fossil fuels is the main driver of carbon pollution and the resultant heating of the planet, and roadmaps to a clean economy require steep, immediate cuts to the supply of coal, oil and gas.

Turkey is far from alone in expanding fossil fuel infrastructure while promising climate action. In recent weeks, co-host Australia granted a licence to restart production at an offshore gasfield, the UK gave the green light to the already-licenced Jackdaw gasfield, and Norway announced a new oil and gas discovery in the North Sea.

Carbon pollution flatlined in 2026, scientists find

Fiona Harvey

Soaring oil and gas prices following the war in Iran have encouraged people to look beyond fossil fuels, leading to an easing of climate-damaging carbon emissions this year.

Carbon dioxide from oil, gas and coal is forecast to flatline for 2026, based on data from the year so far, according to a comprehensive assessment by scientists. Emissions from burning oil alone will drop by 2% as drivers economise on fuel use and flock to electric vehicles instead.

The findings, presented on Tuesday morning at the Cop31 climate talks hosted by Turkey in Antalya, show both the impact of the Iran war and the global expansion of cheap renewable energy, chiefly solar and wind power.

Talk of a global turnaround would be premature, however, the report’s authors and other analysts said. The reduction in emissions from fossil fuels for 2026 will be about 0.4% compared with last year.

Yet this year’s slight fall could be temporary, and was more than offset by increased emissions from deforestation and land use change, following major fires in south-east Asia and further conversions of wild land to agriculture.

Many factors could disrupt the fragile trend of slowing emissions from fossil fuels, including an intensified expansion of coal in India, an easing of oil prices and US president Donald Trump’s enthusiasm for fossil fuels. Much greater investment in renewable energy, and low-carbon technology such as electric vehicles, would still be required to make permanent reductions in annual emissions, the report’s authors said.

In an attempt to get to the venue a bit early, I decided to ditch the tram and try the special Cop31 buses. This was a bad decision.

We have just reached the two-and-a-half-hour mark on the bus and are still crawling through Antalya traffic. New friendships are being spawned in here. We are starting to eat each other’s food.

I want to thank Philippa Bayley from Groundwork for the walnut and chocolate biscuits she snaffled from her hotel buffet.

Exceptional, which is more than I can say for the traffic.

articles.title: Indonesia VP Gibran expresses intent to step down, presidential official says
articles.summary: Presidential spokesperson Prasetyo Hadi denied reports that President Prabowo Subianto rejected Gibran Rakabuming Raka's request, but stopped short of saying the president had accepted it.
articles.preview: Presidential spokesperson Prasetyo Hadi denied reports that President Prabowo Subianto rejected Gibran Rakabuming Raka's request, but stopped short of saying the president had accepted it. JAKARTA: Indonesia's Vice-President Gibran Rakabuming Raka expressed his intention to step down during a meeting on Tuesday (Nov 10) with President Prabowo Subianto, a senior official said, as lawmakers weigh the possibility of a probe into Gibran's eligibility.
articles.body:
Presidential spokesperson Prasetyo Hadi denied reports that President Prabowo Subianto rejected Gibran Rakabuming Raka's request, but stopped short of saying the president had accepted it.

JAKARTA: Indonesia's Vice-President Gibran Rakabuming Raka expressed his intention to step down during a meeting on Tuesday (Nov 10) with President Prabowo Subianto, a senior official said, as lawmakers weigh the possibility of a probe into Gibran's eligibility.

"During the discussion, the vice-president expressed his intention to resign in light of the evolving situation," presidential spokesperson Prasetyo Hadi told reporters.

Prasetyo denied reports that Prabowo rejected Gibran's request, but stopped short of saying the president had accepted it.

The office of the vice-president did not immediately respond to a request for comment.

The meeting came amid a widening political rift between Prabowo and Gibran's influential father, the popular two-term former President Joko Widodo, better known as Jokowi.

Gibran helped Prabowo win the 2024 election by a huge margin, but some lawmakers are seeking to investigate whether incomplete education documents he submitted as a candidate disqualify him as vice president.

Gibran, 39, had kept a low profile as vice-president, and his appearances together with Prabowo have been infrequent in their first two years in office.

But he has been thrust into the spotlight of late as tensions grow between the president and Jokowi, who twice defeated Prabowo in 2014 and 2019 elections before tacitly backing him as his successor.

Lawmakers in parliament, which is overwhelmingly under the control of Prabowo's "big tent" coalition, have been looking into launching an inquiry, which some analysts believe could be the first step towards Gibran's impeachment.

The dispute over Gibran's qualifications came after rulings last month by the Constitutional Court and Supreme Court that the education documents he submitted did not meet election requirements.

The constitutional court, however, said it did not have the power to disqualify him, which was the responsibility of other institutions.

articles.title: French judo star Teddy Riner announces run for presidency
articles.summary: Judy star Teddy Rinner wants to be the next president of France. The 37-year-old Olympic champion announced his bid on social media on Monday. The news comes as polls show the French public largely split between the far-left candidate Jean-Luc Melanchon and the far-right's Marine Le Pen.
articles.preview: Judy star Teddy Rinner wants to be the next president of France. The 37-year-old Olympic champion announced his bid on social media on Monday. The news comes as polls show the French public largely split between the far-left candidate Jean-Luc Melanchon and the far-right's Marine Le Pen.
articles.body:
France

Judo star Teddy Riner wants to be the next French president.

The 37-year-old multiple Olympic champion, who is consistently ranked among France’s favorite public figures, announced his bid on social media on Monday. Riner, who has liberal economic views, said in an interview with Le Parisien newspaper that he is positioning himself as “neither right-wing nor left-wing” and hopes to become a “president who brings people together.”

Asked whether his bid should be taken seriously, Riner said “what would be irresponsible would be to remain silent and stand by as a spectator to what is happening in our country, and what has been happening for several years now.”

The French presidential election is being held next year, and campaigning is taking place in a tense social climate.

Protest marches have been drawing huge crowds for weeks in Paris and elsewhere across France as demonstrators demand higher wages and back the country’s student protest movement, piling fresh pressure on the beleaguered government.

Riner said he is aware of the social tensions running through the country and that he can’t accept young people and older generations saying they are struggling to imagine a future for themselves.

“I hear the anger, which some people echo in their rhetoric with a great deal of negativity, coming from people who no longer have any ambition or the desire to think big,” Riner said. “Yet France is a great country. It has allowed me to become the person I am today and given me the opportunity to dream big. Today, that is precisely what is missing. There is no longer that ambition, no longer that hope.”

Riner said in September that he wants to end his stellar career with a fourth individual Olympic gold medal at the Los Angeles Games in 2028. Asked by Le Parisien if his presidential bid means he is giving up on the Olympics, the 2.04-meter heavyweight said no.

“Not if my duties as president allow it and the French people give me their blessing,” the 11-time world champion said.

French authorities in September said they investigated online racial abuse aimed at Riner after he expressed concern about the rise of the far right. In an interview with French sports television show Stade 2, Riner said he was “freaked out” by the rise of extremism. Asked if he meant “on both sides” — meaning the far left and far right — Riner replied “the far right.”

According to opinion polls, the far-right nationalist Marine Le Pen is the front-runner to replace Emmanuel Macron, ahead of hard-left leader Jean-Luc Mélenchon. Other aspirants include two former prime ministers of Macron. Candidates from the moderate left and right, the Green party and conservatives, are also running, among others.

“The country is experiencing deep divisions right now, let’s not kid ourselves,” Riner said. “And in the face of that, I don’t see a single candidate putting forward a credible and fair vision capable of bringing the French people together rather than dividing them. There is no one today offering genuine, sincere hope. It’s always one side against another. I’m running for president to show that we can get France back on its feet. We are capable of achieving great things together.”

In order to stand, Riner will need to gather 500 sponsorship signatures from elected officials, as required by French law.

Asked about what would be his first initiative on the international stage if he is elected, Riner said he wants to make sure France works well with its allies and commands greater respect.

“A lot of people around me have been talking about my first handshake with Donald Trump,” he said, laughing. “We’ll see who has the firmer handshake.”

articles.title: What powers does Netanyahu have as Israel’s interim PM?
articles.summary: As Israel faces political gridlock, Netanyahu wields caretaker powers to manage security and disrupt his rivals.
articles.preview: As Israel navigates political gridlock, Benjamin Netanyahu retains vast executive authority despite his caretaker status. Two weeks after Israel’s national elections, opposition leader Gadi Eisenkot has been given a chance by President Isaac Herzog to cobble together a government. But with neither Eisenkot nor Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu’s coalition securing the 61 seats needed to secure a majority in the Knesset, who eventually forms the next administration is far from clear.
articles.body:
As Israel navigates political gridlock, Benjamin Netanyahu retains vast executive authority despite his caretaker status.

Two weeks after Israel’s national elections, opposition leader Gadi Eisenkot has been given a chance by President Isaac Herzog to cobble together a government.

But with neither Eisenkot nor Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu’s coalition securing the 61 seats needed to secure a majority in the Knesset, who eventually forms the next administration is far from clear.

As Eisenkot huddles with members of his alliance and negotiates with potential outside partners who could support his coalition, including Arab parties, Netanyahu remains ensconced as a caretaker prime minister. And if Eisenkot fails to form a government, Herzog might approach Netanyahu to see if he can form a workable coalition government.

This transitional status creates a unique political landscape where the incumbent lacks a popular mandate but retains the keys to the state’s most powerful institutions.

“Netanyahu lost the priority of forming the government, but he did not lose the current premiership,” Ehab Jabareen, an analyst and Palestinian citizen of Israel, told Al Jazeera. “His power now lies in that his opponents need an agreement to remove him – and their differences are the reason for his current [political] survival.”

In the meantime, Jabareen explained, Israel sits in a “constitutional paradox”: The prime minister does not enjoy a popular mandate.

So what does that mean for Israel, and what powers does Netanyahu enjoy as a caretaker prime minister?

The big picture

Israel has no single constitution but instead relies on a series of what are known as Basic Laws as its foundational legal principles.

Under Article 30 of Israel’s Basic Law: The Government, the outgoing administration continues to operate seamlessly until there is a new one sworn in to replace it.

“Consequently, Netanyahu and his government continue to work until a new government gains the confidence of the Knesset under the principle of government continuity,” Jabareen said.

“And in this period, the government retains the powers of managing the state, security and foreign relations, but its use is subject to the duty of reservation and restraint.”

Security and war

The most pressing concern surrounding Netanyahu’s caretaker status is his authority over the military.

He has the authority to make new appointments and security-related decisions. But he is expected to face extra scrutiny over any moves because while he has legal powers, he does not necessarily enjoy “legitimacy” any more, Jabareen noted.

While Netanyahu commands the executive branch, Article 40 of the Basic Law: The Government authorises his cabinet to launch a new war if it votes in its favour. He cannot start a new conflict on his own.

But Netanyahu can strategically manipulate existing conflicts. “The most applicable scenario is not inventing a war from scratch, of course. We are talking about igniting and employing an existing threat. We are talking about Iran. We are talking about Lebanon,” Jabareen said.

Because Eisenkot and his allies are not members of the current security cabinet, Netanyahu wields unchecked influence over how intelligence is framed.

“What is presented to the ministers as a danger that can be contained? And what is presented as a final opportunity [for potential attacks] that cannot be delayed? This additional responsibility of the prime minister regarding the information that reaches the cabinet makes the presentation of options extremely important,” Jabareen explained.

The Shin Bet, Israel’s internal intelligence agency, reports directly to the premier. That does not change while Netanyahu is a caretaker prime minister.

Legislative boundaries

While Netanyahu commands security forces, his domestic and legislative powers face functional limits.

Maysara Bahr, a writer and expert on Israeli affairs, explained that financial decisions Netanyahu makes could impact whoever forms the next government.

“Netanyahu can take some actions that may hinder the work of the next government,” so that it inherits greater “indebtedness”, Bahr told Al Jazeera.

However, Netanyahu cannot push through new legislation to protect himself from his long, ongoing corruption trial.

Political manoeuvring

Netanyahu is using his continuing premiership to try to fracture the opposition bloc, Jabareen said.

For instance, the analyst pointed out, Netanyahu is trying to appeal to Zionist voters and parties that represent them by portraying Eisenkot’s alliance as likely to be dependent on Arab parties.

Bahr warned that Netanyahu might encourage domestic unrest to derail the transition, suggesting that the prime minister would do whatever it takes to try to stay in power.

How Israel’s transition compares to other countries

Israel’s transition process is not very different from that in other parliamentary democracies.

In the United Kingdom and India too, for instance, caretaker prime ministers enjoy the same legal powers as premiers with electoral mandates.

However, constitutional conventions and norms require them to avoid major policy decisions – including on questions of war – as caretakers.

In the United States, meanwhile, an outgoing president works under a rigid two-and-a-half-month deadline towards the inauguration of his successor, facing intense congressional oversight regarding transitions, budgets and appointments in the interim.

articles.title: Trump says FBI investigating Nvidia boss's affair with alleged Chinese spy
articles.summary: The US president said he spoke with Jensen Huang on Monday and asked him about the affair with the alleged spy.
articles.preview: US President Donald Trump has said the FBI is investigating the affair between the chief executive of Nvidia and an alleged Chinese spy. Trump said he spoke to Jensen Huang on Monday following reports that the US believed he had been targeted in a Chinese espionage campaign. "I asked him that question, 'Did you have any idea she was a spy?' He said 'I had no idea she was a spy' and I really believe him," Trump told reporters.
articles.body:
US President Donald Trump has said the FBI is investigating the affair between the chief executive of Nvidia and an alleged Chinese spy.

Trump said he spoke to Jensen Huang on Monday following reports that the US believed he had been targeted in a Chinese espionage campaign.

"I asked him that question, 'Did you have any idea she was a spy?' He said 'I had no idea she was a spy' and I really believe him," Trump told reporters.

Beijing has rejected claims that Huang was targeted, with its foreign ministry saying the allegations were "entirely groundless, speculative and intended to smear and malign China".

Speaking later at a White House press briefing, Trump told reporters, "I know the FBI is looking into" the affair but did not give further details on the investigation, or confirm when it was launched.

Trump added he thought that Huang was an "honourable guy and I feel very confident that he will be in good shape" after the investigations.

The FBI declined to comment when contacted by the BBC.

Nvidia, which has commissioned an independent investigation into the affair involving Alice Huang, alleged to be a Chinese spy, said it had no reason to believe the company's secrets or national security were compromised.

Nvidia is the world's second most valuable company after Apple, and designs computer chips that have become central to AI technology.

The revelations knocked about $250bn (£190bn) off Nvidia's value on Monday as the company's share price fell by more than 4%.

US intelligence officials believe Alice Huang, also known as Huang Le, was a spy for Beijing, according to a New York Times report. She is not related to Jensen Huang.

According to the newspaper, Secretary of State Marco Rubio sent a memo to top officials in Washington in spring this year, warning that the Nvidia boss was in a close relationship with a Chinese spy.

- What we know so far about Jensen Huang's affair with suspected Chinese spy

- Published9 hours ago

- Nvidia shares tumble over investigation into Huang's affair with alleged Chinese spy

- Published13 hours ago

Alice Huang was managing director of Singaporean company Megaspeed, which has had dealings with Nvidia.

Trump's remarks are the first indication of whether Nvidia's Huang knew about the woman's alleged ties to Chinese espionage.

Megaspeed's office in Singapore's central business district appeared to be operational and staffed on Tuesday.

The BBC was refused entry to its floor, but spoke to a staff member by phone who said they had no comment and directed all queries to the company's PR team.

The BBC has emailed Megaspeed several times for comment.

Nvidia, co-founded by Jensen Huang, is also a major focus in the AI technology race between the US and China, with officials in Washington treating its exports to Beijing as a matter of national security - a key reason why Huang's affair has sparked concerns.

Also on Monday, Huang and Nvidia were sued in a proposed class action lawsuit in California that accuses them of defrauding shareholders by concealing his ties with the suspected Chinese spy.

The lawsuit alleges that the company lied to the media about Jensen Huang's relationship with Alice Huang, "who is suspected of seeking to help smuggle Nvidia products to China."

The BBC has contacted Nvidia for comment on the lawsuit.

'An honourable guy'

At the White House, Trump was asked several times when he was made aware of the relationship. He said he was informed "over a period of time" but was not specific.

"I hope there's no problem, I believe he is suffering greatly," the president added.

He said he spoke to Huang on the phone on Monday "just to see if he's feeling alright, how you doing and I asked him about that and he said he absolutely had no idea that the person in question was a spy".

Trump has raised concerns that allowing China to lead in AI would supercharge Beijing's military and surveillance capabilities.

The president added he was "sure" Chinese leader Xi Jinping would "ask me about it" when they next met.

Huang has admitted that he was "unfaithful" to his wife and apologised for hurting her and their children.

He said on Monday that he was "committed to protecting Nvidia and supporting America's national security" and would cooperate with the investigation the company had launched.

Huang has also been requested to appear for a joint closed-door briefing for several Congressional committees next week, however it is unclear whether Huang will appear.

A letter said the briefing would be "on Nvidia's security protocols against foreign adversary espionage and your interactions with a publicly reported People's Republic of China (PRC) intelligence asset: Megaspeed executive Alice Huang".

Nvidia has declined to comment, while the the BBC has also contacted the committees.

- Zoe Kleinman: Nvidia CEO's affair will cause ripples across US and beyond

- Published11 hours ago

- AI stocks climb after trillions wiped from market values

- Published3 days ago

Some workers the BBC spoke to at Nvidia's Santa Clara headquarters on Monday said it was business as usual, despite the intense attention on the company.

Nvidia has been around for decades, with Huang founding it with two other engineers in 1993, but its rise to one of the world's most valuable and powerful companies has only been recent.

It originally designed computer chips for gaming, but its decision to shift focus to AI development turned it into the powerhouse it is today.

Its chips have become so valuable to the AI buildout that the White House previously imposed controls on where its advanced products could be sold.

The H200, Nvidia's second most advanced semiconductor, had previously been restricted over concerns that it would give China's technology industry an edge over the US.

But Huang has long been against restricting sales to China, arguing that it would be better for the global rollout of AI to be powered by US technology.

In January, the Trump administration said it would allow the company to sell its H200 chips to Chinese customers under certain conditions.

Nvidia's most advanced AI semiconductors including the GB200 Blackwell super chip remain blocked from the Chinese market.

articles.body:
Paul Biya

Cameroonian President Paul Biya, the world's oldest head of state, announced on Monday that legislative and local elections will be held on February 7 - the first ballots since the veteran leader was reelected in contested polls last year.

Biya, 93, has ruled the country since 1982, but his reelection was rejected by the opposition and led to demonstrations bloodily suppressed by the authorities.

The new polls come in a tense political context, marked by the repression of the opposition and the inertia of those in power at the top of the state.

The announcement was made in a decree read on public radio and follows two postponements of the elections.

The country is awaiting a government reshuffle announced nearly a year ago, as well as the appointment of a vice president, a position reintroduced by a constitutional reform in April, who would be expected to succeed Biya in the event of his death.

Biya's frequent trips abroad are fuelling debate about his state of health and his ability to lead the country.

At the end of August, Biya returned to Yaounde after spending more than two months in Geneva, Switzerland, provoking sharp criticism from the opposition.

Last month the authorities suspended the Cameroon National Salvation Front (FSNC), the party of defeated opposition presidential candidate Issa Tchiroma Bakary.

Bakary went into exile in the Gambia after declaring himself the winner of the election, and calling on supporters to defend his "victory", triggering protests.

articles.title: Japan to call for limiting children’s exposure to social media
articles.summary: A government draft says schools should help children develop their judgment so that they can use social media appropriately.
articles.preview: Upcoming government guidelines are expected to say that parents and other guardians should limit the exposure of young children to social media and other internet content, a draft showed Tuesday. The draft, created by the Children and Families Agency, outlined key issues that need to be discussed to complete the guidelines for setting up an appropriate environment for children to use social media services and the internet.
articles.body:
Upcoming government guidelines are expected to say that parents and other guardians should limit the exposure of young children to social media and other internet content, a draft showed Tuesday.

The draft, created by the Children and Families Agency, outlined key issues that need to be discussed to complete the guidelines for setting up an appropriate environment for children to use social media services and the internet.

During early childhood up to age 2, a critical period for the development of children’s minds and bodies, parents should select the content their children view and ensure they do not spend excessive time using digital services, the draft said.

In the draft, the agency divided children up to age 18 into six age groups and outlined precautions for each, saying that children’s interactions with social media and the online environments for them change with age.

The agency hopes that specific measures will be discussed at expert panel meetings and elsewhere to establish the guidelines to protect children from risks related to social media and other online services.

For children age zero to 2, the draft said that priority should be given to direct interactions with other people, stressing that parents should assess the purpose and necessity of their children’s use of social media and other digital services.

For those age 6 to 9, who begin using devices for educational purposes, the draft proposed providing more opportunities for them to think independently and make choices for themselves in a safe online environment.

For those age 13 to 15, who become more active in interactions on social media, the draft said that parents should respect children’s independence and privacy rather than trying to fully manage their online activities.

Schools should help children develop their judgment so that they can use social media appropriately, the draft said, calling on service providers to establish systems that children can use easily to seek advice and report problems.

BEIJING – China’s trade surplus surged past $1 trillion in the first 10 months of 2026 as a global race to build artificial intelligence infrastructure buoyed sales of high-tech products and helped offset weak domestic demand, a dynamic likely to sharpen tensions with major trading partners.

The data comes ahead of next week’s Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation summit in Shenzhen, where Chinese President Xi Jinping and U.S. President Donald Trump are expected to meet for the third time this year, putting broader economic ties and tariff policy squarely in focus.

The figures highlight Beijing’s growing reliance on overseas demand to support an economy hobbled by subdued consumption and a protracted property slump. But while the global AI investment boom is expected to keep demand for Chinese technology products strong into 2027, analysts warn that deeper dependence on external markets could leave China more vulnerable to protectionist measures abroad while masking persistent weakness at home.

articles.body:
The first major storm of the season flooded about 70,000 tents in Gaza within 12 hours, killing at least five people and causing about $3m in damage, according to Gaza’s Government Media Office.

The storm hit over the weekend. By Monday, Gaza’s Civil Defence had logged more than 2,100 distress calls, warning that more than 2,000 buildings risk collapse. Nearly 400,000 displaced people shelter in areas judged highly vulnerable.

Israel is blocking 60,000 mobile homes and 200,000 tents, allowing only 20,000 tents into Gaza, where about 85 percent of homes have been destroyed or damaged by Israel’s three-year genocidal war.

Gaza’s Crossings and Borders Authority said Israel also let in no aid trucks or commercial goods on November 6 and 7; five trucks of cooking gas entered the next day. The UN’s Office for the Coordination of Humanitarian Affairs (OCHA) says Israel notified the UN on November 1 that it would suspend shipments from Egypt, and aid groups warn daily cooked meals could fall from about 600,000 to 330,000 as a result.

Gaza’s Ministry of Health says 20 more Palestinians were killed over the past week, bringing the toll since the October 2025 “ceasefire” to 1,613 as of November 9. Among them:

- Storm collapse, November 8: A sand embankment fell onto tents at a displacement site southwest of Deir el-Balah. Five bodies were recovered, among them Tahrir Nabhan and her daughter Maryam, and Habiba al-Zein.

- Strikes and shootings: On November 3, Rimas al-Madhoun, 16, was killed in a strike on a tent in Gaza City. Two days later, Noura Sheikh al-Eid was killed by tank fire in al-Mawasi hours after her daughter left for treatment in Egypt, and 12-year-old Adnan al-Qirnawi was shot and killed east of Bureij the same day. Nermin al-Amour and Mahmoud Abu Hammad were then killed on November 8 in a Khan Younis strike.

The weekend storm came as Hamas urged mediators and the Board of Peace not to link reconstruction to political or security conditions.

Arab-led parties at the table, and in the crosshairs

The political battle over Gaza’s future is unfolding as parties representing Palestinian citizens of Israel hold potentially decisive leverage in Israel’s post-election negotiations – amid an ongoing demonisation campaign against the parties and Arab voting power in Israel.

President Isaac Herzog gave opposition leader Gadi Eisenkot the mandate to form a government over the weekend after 67 members of parliament recommended him, against 46 for Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu.

Eisenkot wants a “national emergency government” open to any party accepting four principles, including recognition of Israel as a “Jewish and democratic” state, and Hamas as a “terrorist” group to be destroyed. For his part, Netanyahu gave a speech seeking a “national unity” government with Eisenkot, Likud, and his Haredi and far-right allies, warning that a government reliant on Arab-led parties would be backed by those who “want to eliminate Israel”.

One of the Arab-led blocs, the Joint List, has said its priority is to topple the Netanyahu government, but that it cannot join an administration that violates international law. It has also said it expects action on education, welfare and crime if it is to support Eisenkot from outside government.

In discussions with Herzog, Mansour Abbas, the leader of the other Arab-led party, the United Arab List (Ra’am), declined to call Hamas a “terror” group, citing fear for his family, while backing its disarmament, according to the Times of Israel. Avigdor Liberman, leader of the opposition Yisrael Beytenu party, repeated that no government should rely on either Palestinian-led party.

Beyond the rhetoric, journalist Abed Abou Shhadeh, a Palestinian citizen of Israel, was released without charge on November 8 after five days in the custody of the domestic intelligence agency, the Shin Bet, saying his arrest was meant “to intimidate Arab society as a whole”.

The Shin Bet chief sought to question leaders of the Palestinian-led parties, but Israel’s attorney general says the fraud probes would not “even remotely” change the result of the election. Tensions on the streets led to a far-right march through a Palestinian neighbourhood in the mixed city of al-Lyd (Lod) on the evening of November 8, which ended in a brawl and 11 arrests, according to the Times of Israel.

West Bank: Takeovers, seizures and a harvest under attack

On November 4, about 30 settlers backed by the settler group Nachala entered Ein a-Duyuk a-Tahta, near Jericho, and took over eight Palestinian homes. Peace Now, citing reports, said settlers shot a Palestinian man in the leg, and the UN said the army declared a closed military zone, blocking humanitarian access.

Settlers say they bought the homes through Nachala; Jericho Governor Hussein Hamayel called the sale a forgery.

For months, the state has backed settlers’ land razing and takeover efforts in the area, and that continued this week. The Jerusalem Post reported the alleged purchase was coordinated with the settler Binyamin Regional Council.

Haaretz reported that Central Command chief Major General Avi Bluth knew of the entry in advance and told the settlers not to alert senior officers until they were inside, with three army platoons diverted to protect the settlers during the takeover of houses; the army called the Haaretz report false.

But Jericho was only the most dramatic case of a multi-pronged escalation in which land seizures, demolitions, attacks and arrests unfolded in the West Bank, with settlers, soldiers and the Civil Administration often working in concert.

- Attacks on the olive harvest: OCHA counts 377 harvest-related attacks since September 1, more than any previous season. In October alone, OCHA documented 457 attacks causing casualties or damage in the West Bank, the most in any month since it began counting in 2006. In Burqa, northwest of Ramallah, settlers set olive groves on fire on November 5 while forces stopped residents from putting them out. Near Salfit, settlers beat three young men with clubs on November 8, and on November 9 they drove farmers off land near Silwad and injured one near Tayasir, according to Palestinian state news agency Wafa.

- Demolitions: On November 4, forces demolished 21 structures belonging to three families in the northern Jordan Valley and five homes in Biddu the next day. On November 9, according to Wafa, a 200-square-metre house, its well and fruit trees were razed in al-Hijra, near Dura.

- Sieges and closures: Settlers entered the sixth week of a nearly complete siege of Yusuf Shanaran’s home in Wadi al-Rakheem, according to Shanaran. According to village mayor Marwan Sabah, a similar settler siege continues of the Abayet family home in Umm Safa, which recently received demolition orders from the Israeli Civil Administration, despite it being built before Israel’s occupation began in 1967. In the south, forces closed Hebron’s Ibrahimi Mosque to Palestinians for two days during a Jewish holiday, days after the army ended a 10-day operation in the city.

articles.body:
G7 foreign ministers are meeting in Paris ahead of the US-mediated Russia-Ukraine talks in Abu Dhabi.

European foreign ministers have told United States Secretary of State Marco Rubio that Europe must have a say in any deal to end Russia’s war on Ukraine, as US-mediated peace talks get under way in Abu Dhabi.

They made the appeal on Monday in Paris, at a meeting of foreign ministers from the Group of Seven, which includes Canada, France, Germany, Italy, Japan, the United Kingdom and the United States.

It was Rubio’s first meeting with allies since last week’s midterm elections, in which President Donald Trump’s Republican Party suffered stunning losses. The meeting gave Washington’s allies a chance to air their concerns with Rubio directly amid concern about Trump’s growing rhetoric of a new security architecture for Europe.

“It is certainly neither necessary, nor right, nor appropriate to make a fundamental change” to Europe’s security architecture, said German Minister for Foreign Affairs Johann Wadephul after talks with Rubio.

“Europe belongs at this table. There can be no solution without Europe – only with Europe,” he added.

The two-day Paris meeting, which ends on Tuesday, overlaps with the talks between Russia and Ukraine, scheduled for Tuesday and Wednesday.

Wadephul said the Abu Dhabi talks must show whether Russia is “genuinely prepared to negotiate”, urging Moscow to “give up maximalist demands” and warning against any “negotiation show” in the capital of the United Arab Emirates.

With Russian attacks on Ukraine’s civilian infrastructure continuing, he said, “we see no substantial contribution whatsoever toward negotiations gaining any serious momentum” from Moscow.

Andrii Sybiha, Ukraine’s foreign minister, is set to join a session on Ukraine in Paris on Tuesday.

“No one has the right to decide our fate behind our backs,” Sybiha said before departing for the meeting.

The Paris meeting comes as G7 members have grown increasingly uneasy with the direction of US policy, including Washington’s scaling back of support for Ukraine and of sanctions on Russia, as well as its increasingly unilateral course.

Ministers from Saudi Arabia, Egypt, South Korea and Brazil are also attending.

Iran is expected to feature prominently in the discussions on Tuesday.

Washington’s G7 allies have repeatedly voiced scepticism about the US and Israeli war on Iran and fear that further US military action could deepen the crisis rather than resolve it.

Al Jazeera’s Rebecca Collard, reporting from Paris, said the first day of talks had wrapped up with little clarity on US policy after the midterm elections.

“The second day of talks will include a session on instability in the Middle East,” she said.

“But there is something bigger up for discussion, too: The future of the multilateralism that has dominated relations among these countries for decades.”

articles.body:
Due giorni nella vita di due persone innamorate. Il primo, quando tutto comincia, e l’ultimo, quando ci si lascia. A chi legge, la possibilità di immaginare cosa è successo in mezzo. In questa puntata: : Paul, 30 anni.

Il primo giorno

“Era l’epoca in cui Tinder era completamente gratuito e io mettevo like a tutti i profili senza pensarci troppo, in piena modalità rimorchio. Per quanto riguarda le mie foto, ho un profilo orientato al marketing: mi si vede sullo skate, vestito da medico o su una scogliera con lo sguardo da amante della natura. Sotto ci scrivo sempre frasi un po’ assurde, come ‘in rivolta permanente’ o ‘il cassetto è nella chiave’, che fanno più intellettuale che medico. Un giorno faccio match con una bellissima ragazza bionda dal viso d’angelo. Sulla sua prima foto abbraccia un gatto così forte da strangolarlo. In un’altra, posa come una modella. Nella biografia cita scrittori russi.

È lei che mi contatta per prima, cosa rara per una ragazza. All’improvviso mi dice che ha voglia di incontrarmi perché sta scrivendo un articolo sulle persone che rimorchiano su Tinder. Cerco su internet, capisco che ha davvero una fanzine di moda. Passiamo due settimane a parlare di letteratura, di arte, comincio a essere preso da questa giovane ragazza super intelligente, che mi ha divertito, mentre di solito mi annoio, anche perché in ospedale non si parla d’altro che del tempo che fa e delle sbronze con gli amici.

Alla fine decidiamo di incontrarci per una mostra al Museo d’arte moderna di Strasburgo. Andavo quasi tutti i giorni a fare skate con i miei amici sul piazzale davanti al museo. Quando arriva, sono tutti curiosi quanto me di vedere com’è. E in effetti è molto bella, non mi sorride, mi analizza, rimane sulla difensiva.

A corto di banalità, usciamo dal museo guardandoci negli occhi come due liceali. A dire il vero, lei va ancora al liceo. Ci sediamo su una panchina del quartiere della Petite France e comincia a piovere come nei film. La gente corre in tutte le direzioni, gli impiegati si coprono la testa con le loro valigette. Le prendo la mano, poi ci baciamo per dieci minuti.

Sull’app Note del mio iPhone ho un elenco delle ragazze con cui vado a letto. A volte non so neanche come si chiamano, in quel caso scrivo ‘ragazza della scala’ o ‘dentro l’ascensore’. Ma sto cambiando le mie abitudini. Le faccio una proposta piuttosto classica, un tè a casa mia – di solito il tè funziona bene, dà l’impressione di un ragazzo rassicurante, che legge libri mentre sorseggia una bevanda calda. L’acqua si riscalda, ma non abbiamo il tempo di metterci dentro la bustina. Dopo lei torna a casa, dai genitori che la aspettano. La vedo andare via e penso che questa volta è una cosa importante. Che mi avrebbe tirato fuori quel ‘ti amo’ che non riuscivo a dire”.

L’ultimo giorno

“Gare de l’Est a Parigi, sono parcheggiato in seconda fila, sono venuto a prenderla per portarla in Bretagna. Arriva con degli occhiali da sole che le coprono tutto il viso e lasciano fuori solo le labbra dipinte di rosso vivo. Con un’aria da modella di cattivo umore, appena metto la valigia nel bagagliaio mi accusa di non essere abbastanza contento di vederla. In realtà ho il mio solito atteggiamento indolente. Lei cerca subito lo scontro.

Non apre bocca per tutto il viaggio in autostrada, fino al cartello che indica Chartres. Le propongo di andare a vedere la cattedrale. Da quando vado in vacanza a Saint-Brieuc, non mi sono mai fermato a visitarla. Entriamo in città, mentre parcheggiamo lei trova un capello biondo sul sedile. Mi fa una scenata di gelosia anche se, questa volta, il capello è di mia madre. Furiosa, sbatte la porta e si incammina per Chartres con la sua valigia rossa. Le ruote saltellano sul selciato, le corro dietro, la rassicuro, lei prova a credermi. ‘Te lo giuro, è di mia madre’.

Continuiamo a passeggiare per Chartres, la città è carina, le compro un croissant alle mandorle, il suo dolce preferito. Ci rimettiamo in marcia. Al volante le dico delle parole che non penso, la situazione lo richiede. C’è qualcosa di assoluto nel ‘ti amo’, che mi dà fastidio. Di solito preferisco comportarmi da stronzo, almeno non si rimane delusi. Arriviamo a Pléneuf-Val-André. La casa sulla spiaggia fa il suo effetto, ma il clima di fiducia non si ristabilisce. Lei comincia a farmi una scenata dopo l’altra, non mi dà tregua. Una notte la bacio prima di andare a dormire e la trovo brutta, puzza di sigarette e di sudore. Mi chiudo in camera.

Grida in continuazione, non capisco perché sia voluta venire in Bretagna. Bussa più volte alla porta. L’immagino come una strega, la mia anima non la venera più, è una doccia fredda, come la pioggia del primo giorno ma al contrario. Quella notte decido che non voglio più sentir parlare di lei, come se fosse una storia di una notte finita male.

All’alba, dopo la mia notte chiuso in stanza, la trovo addormentata sul divano. La valigia ai suoi piedi, mezza disfatta, come a dire: ‘Vado via, ma tu trattienimi’. Lei si sveglia, si accende una sigaretta e mi lancia un’occhiata. All’improvviso scappa di casa e si mette a correre a piedi nudi sulla spiaggia, interrompendo gli esercizi degli sportivi delle prime ore del giorno. Mi prende le mani, mi dice che mi ama, che se ne andrà. Le dico che sì, deve andare via.

Torniamo a casa e ridiventa più tranquilla, non credo che voglia davvero andarsene. Vuole fare l’amore, ma io le faccio la valigia. Non dice più nulla, saliamo in macchina e andiamo alla stazione. Come gesto di disperazione, fa accostare l’auto e scappa correndo nel campo vicino alla strada – ha corso parecchio quel giorno. La vedo che si nasconde dietro a un cespuglio, prende il telefono e mi chiama. Lo lascio squillare e lei mi lascia un messaggio in cui mi ripete che mi ama.

Ma io non cedo, arriviamo alla stazione di Saint-Brieuc, sono le 10 di mattina e non ho alcuna idea degli orari dei treni. La lascio sul marciapiede accanto ai binari e decido che non mi interessa più niente di quello che le succederà. Lei è là e io provo odio. Ero davvero innamorato di lei”.

(Traduzione di Andrea De Ritis)

Amore che vieni, amore che vai è una serie del quotidiano francese Le Monde che racconta il primo e l’ultimo giorno di una storia d’amore. Qui ci sono tutte le puntate.

For Palestinians in Gaza, if the bombs don’t get them, the floods, famine and disease will. Taking a lead In Israel, the governing coalition led by Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu has resorted to its usual blame game , saying it’s all Hamas’s fault. Israel, however, can take action - and importantly, it has an international legal obligation, as the occupying power, to care for the people in the territory it occupies. In a statement , it called on the Israeli government to “authorize and facilitate the entry of all necessary winterization and humanitarian supplies”. Gaza genocide: How Israel made horror a ritual of daily life , which was their standard operating procedure for years, even before the genocide. They cannot - and must not - defer action until the arcane process of Israeli coalition-building and political chicanery glues together the next fractious Israeli government. Sanctions have been, and remain, a requirement. With most other states, in the event of mass collective punishment of hundreds of thousands of civilians, a ream of ever-tightening bans and sanctions would be issued by European states. The United Kingdom can take a lead. It recently amended its Global Human Rights and International Humanitarian Law Sanctions Regulations to allow the UK government to sanction those who block humanitarian aid. Gaza is the perfect example of a situation where these sanctions need to be invoked, as dozens of politicians argued in a letter to Foreign Secretary Ed Miliband last month. Other states must adopt similar measures immediately. Thousands of Palestinian lives are at stake in a situation that can easily be relieved. It is time to break the terrible record of consistently failing Palestinian men, women and children, which has tarnished the international record for so long. articles.summary: Air-raid sirens signaling the threat of missile or drone strikes have become a daily occurrence for millions of residents in most of central Russia.

articles.body:
Olga was jolted awake by an explosion so powerful that her apartment building shuddered and the windows and furniture shook. Looking outside, she saw a plume of thick black smoke rising from a military equipment factory that had just been hit by a missile.

Residents panicked, said Olga, a 49-year-old choreographer. “We didn’t know whether we should run to a shelter,” she said. The strike on the plant left six people dead and another 26 injured, according to the local governor.

Olga doesn’t live in Kyiv, Kherson or any other Ukrainian city that’s been pounded for years by Russian President Vladimir Putin’s forces. This is Kirov, a Russian city about 800 kilometers northeast of Moscow known for its 16th century onion-domed monastery rather than being in a war zone.

articles.title: Gli Stati Uniti sbilanciano le trattative tra russi e ucraini
articles.summary: I rappresentati dei due paesi in guerra sono ad Abu Dhabi per il primo incontro formale da febbraio dell’anno scorso. Ma l’accondiscendenza di Trump verso Putin non fa ben sperare
articles.preview: Il 10 novembre russi e ucraini si ritrovano faccia a faccia ad Abu Dhabi, negli Emirati Arabi Uniti, per il primo incontro formale da febbraio dell’anno scorso. Insieme a loro ci sono Steve Witkoff e Jared Kushner, gli inviati di Donald Trump. Gli europei sono stati consultati, ma resteranno comunque esclusi dal dialogo. Ancora una volta emerge il solito interrogativo: è possibile fermare questa guerra che dura da quasi cinque anni e ha provocato un’ecatombe?
articles.body:
Il 10 novembre russi e ucraini si ritrovano faccia a faccia ad Abu Dhabi, negli Emirati Arabi Uniti, per il primo incontro formale da febbraio dell’anno scorso. Insieme a loro ci sono Steve Witkoff e Jared Kushner, gli inviati di Donald Trump. Gli europei sono stati consultati, ma resteranno comunque esclusi dal dialogo.

Ancora una volta emerge il solito interrogativo: è possibile fermare questa guerra che dura da quasi cinque anni e ha provocato un’ecatombe? Secondo i dati dell’istituto di statistica russo, rubati e diffusi da un gruppo di hacker, i morti sul fronte russo sarebbero 400mila, mentre le ultime stime parlano di 100mila vittime ucraine. Per non dire delle sofferenze di un popolo intero, che si appresta a trascorrere l’inverno più duro dall’inizio del conflitto.

Gli unici a volere un accordo a tutti i costi sono gli inviati di Trump. Il presidente statunitense, infatti, ha subìto una sconfitta elettorale umiliante e ha bisogno di cancellare l’immagine di loser, perdente. Il problema è che Trump appare del tutto accondiscendente nei confronti del presidente russo Vladimir Putin, come dimostra il fatto che alla vigilia dell’incontro abbia continuato ad attaccare quello ucraino, Volodymyr Zelenskyj, accusandolo di “mancanza di rispetto” nei confronti della Russia, senza criticare minimamente i bombardamenti dell’esercito russo contro obiettivi civili.

Tutto questo non lascia certo presagire una soluzione rapida, tanto più che Putin sembra convinto di poter piegare durante l’inverno la resistenza ucraina, approfittando delle difficoltà della difesa aerea del nemico e dei danni inflitti alle infrastrutture civili. Quasi ogni giorno la Russia compie azioni che costituirebbero crimini di guerra se solo il diritto internazionale umanitario fosse minimamente rispettato. Putin, però, può contare sulla debolezza degli europei e sulla certezza che Trump chiuderà un occhio.

Il presidente russo è sicuramente entusiasta davanti allo spettacolo delle divisioni europee, a cominciare dai sondaggi francesi che indicano come favoriti per il secondo turno due candidati che, ognuno a modo suo, indebolirebbero il sostegno all’Ucraina. Marine Le Pen ha dichiarato che la Francia “non ha più i mezzi” per assistere Kiev, mentre Jean-Luc Mélenchon propone un referendum nelle zone del Donbass controllate dall’esercito russo.

Il 9 novembre Kiev ha risposto al candidato della France insoumise ricordando il referendum del 1991 con cui l’83 per cento degli abitanti del Donbass votò per l’indipendenza, aggiungendo che “i referendum sotto occupazione sono uno strumento di annessione, non un’espressione della volontà popolare. Nessun paese civile e democratico accetterebbe questo processo per stabilire i suoi confini”.

L’Ucraina può sperare che la presenza degli europei ad Abu Dhabi, anche se nell’anticamera degli incontri e non al tavolo dei negoziati, possa scongiurare un tradimento troppo clamoroso. Di recente i rappresentanti del continente sono rimasti sconvolti quando hanno scoperto (all’ultimo minuto) che Trump aveva deciso di cancellare le sanzioni contro la Russia nel tentativo, poi risultato inutile, di far abbassare il prezzo del petrolio e limitare le perdite alle elezioni di metà mandato.

Per gli ucraini il nuovo parlamento statunitense, che si insedierà all’inizio di gennaio, è una buona notizia, perché vigilerà sull’applicazione delle sanzioni adottate in primavera su iniziativa del senatore repubblicano Lindsey Graham, morto poco dopo. Di sicuro il nuovo congresso sarà meno incline a favorire Putin.

Intanto il teatro pseudodiplomatico si sposta ad Abu Dhabi. Tuttavia, il tentativo di relegare la guerra in Ucraina all’ombra di un’altra guerra, quella in Iran, che Trump non riesce a risolvere, non lascia molto spazio all’ottimismo.

(Traduzione di Andrea Sparacino)

articles.title: US moves aircraft from second UK base over ‘threat from Iran’
articles.summary: Two refuelling tankers and several other aircraft diverted from RAF Mildenhall airbase ​to other locations, WSJ reports.
articles.preview: The United States military has moved aircraft from a second airbase in the United Kingdom “in the wake of a threat from Iran”, The Wall Street Journal reported, citing people familiar with the matter. Two US refuelling tankers and several other tankers that were using the RAF Mildenhall military base in eastern England diverted to Germany and other locations on Monday, the WSJ reported on Tuesday. The report said the precise nature of the threat to RAF Mildenhall remains under discussion among US officials.
articles.body:
The United States military has moved aircraft from a second airbase in the United Kingdom “in the wake of a threat from Iran”, The Wall Street Journal reported, citing people familiar with the matter.

Two US refuelling tankers and several other tankers that were using the RAF Mildenhall military base in eastern England diverted to Germany and other locations on Monday, the WSJ reported on Tuesday.

The report said the precise nature of the threat to RAF Mildenhall remains under discussion among US officials.

The US upgraded the security posture at RAF Mildenhall and RAF Lakenheath to Force Protection Condition (FPCON) Charlie, the WSJ report said, quoting a US official familiar with the matter.

FPCON Charlie is the second-highest defensive threat level in the US Department of Defense’s security system and occurs when intelligence indicates that a form of “terrorist” action is likely.

“We do not routinely comment on the activity of other nations,” a UK Ministry of Defence spokesperson said in a statement.

“Aircraft and other assets move regularly according to operational requirements.”

A US Air Force spokesperson said aircraft rotate between installations and operating locations for various reasons.

The report comes weeks after five men were arrested outside RAF Fairford airbase in southwest England over a security incident, with two others arrested later on suspicion of assisting Iranian intelligence.

The circumstances of the September incident remain largely unexplained, but it prompted the US to remove its B-1 bombers from the airbase on security grounds.

It came at a time of heightened concern about the wider security implications of the US-Israel war on Iran.

RAF Fairford had been used by US bombers that carried out strikes on Iran.

British Prime Minister Andy Burnham said last month that the activity at RAF Fairford was likely to have been coordinated in Iran.

While Tehran’s ambassador to the UK has denied accusations that it was involved in any plot against the airbase, the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps said in July that Fairford and any other base used to launch attacks against Iran were legitimate targets.

articles.title: Khor Mor drone attack raises fears over Iraq’s energy security
articles.summary: Drone strike disrupts electricity supply in Iraq's semi-autonomous Kurdish region, renewing concerns about armed groups.
articles.preview: Drone strike disrupts electricity supplies in the semi-autonomous Kurdish region of northern Iraq, renewing concerns about armed groups. A drone attack on the Khor Mor gasfield in the semi-autonomous Kurdish region of northern Iraq has drawn attention to the security challenges facing the country’s energy sector, amid escalating regional tensions and domestic political disagreements over restricting weapons to state control.
articles.body:
Drone strike disrupts electricity supplies in the semi-autonomous Kurdish region of northern Iraq, renewing concerns about armed groups.

A drone attack on the Khor Mor gasfield in the semi-autonomous Kurdish region of northern Iraq has drawn attention to the security challenges facing the country’s energy sector, amid escalating regional tensions and domestic political disagreements over restricting weapons to state control.

The attack in Sulaimaniyah governorate late on Sunday sparked a fire and forced the suspension of gas supplies to several power stations, initially reducing electricity generation in areas administered by the Kurdistan Regional Government (KRG) by between 2,500 and 2,800 megawatts, according to regional officials.

Iraqi Prime Minister Ali al-Zaidi has ordered the formation of a joint investigative committee with KRG authorities to determine who was behind the attack.

No group has claimed responsibility, but the attack comes as regional tensions are heightened due to the US-Israel war on Iran, with Baghdad facing pressure to bring weapons held by predominantly pro-Iranian Shia armed factions under state control. KRG authorities have blamed Iran-backed groups in Iraq for previous attacks on the field in recent years.

The attack also comes days after the Patriotic Union of Kurdistan (PUK) announced its withdrawal from the KRG, deepening a political crisis with its rival, the Kurdistan Democratic Party (KDP).

Test of Iraqi sovereignty

Mohammed Amer, a political science academic and a member of the KDP, said the Khor Mor attack represents a genuine test of the Iraqi state’s sovereignty and its ability to rein in armed groups operating outside its control, and protect its territory and vital facilities.

“The [federal Iraqi] government bears responsibility for protecting Iraqi territory and airspace,” Amer told Al Jazeera. “The repeated targeting of energy sources in the Kurdistan Region also requires it to hold accountable the parties and factions behind these attacks, and to question the authorities responsible for the areas from which they are launched.”

Amer urged the Iraqi government to accelerate efforts to bring weapons under state control, warning that repeated attacks coud deter foreign investment in Iraq’s energy industry.

“These strikes target foreign investment in Iraq’s energy sector, particularly as the Khor Mor field has been targeted many times using drones and missiles,” he said. “There are factions that declare their loyalty to Iran and not to the Iraqi state, and this raises questions about the government’s ability to impose its authority and sovereignty over all Iraqi territory.”

Strategic affairs researcher Kadhim Yawer also linked the attack to regional tensions, with fears continuing that the war between the United States and Iran may escalate once again in the coming days and weeks.

“The strategic purpose of targeting the Khor Mor field at this time is primarily due to external factors linked to the escalation of the conflict between Iran and the US, as well as the desire to inflict economic damage on the Kurdistan Region and Iraq in general,” Yawer said.

He said that the dispute over disarming militias, combined with worsening divisions between the KDP and the PUK, could add to the economic pressure on the region. That comes at a time when, according to Yawer, the field’s importance could grow as the KRG seeks to expand gas production and potentially reach new markets.

Yawer argued that the withdrawal of US-led coalition forces from Iraq had created additional security challenges, particularly as some political forces – including parliamentarians – continue to not support the full disarmament of militias, allowing them more freedom to operate.

Internal disputes raise fears of wider conflict

Political researcher Ghanem al-Abed pointed to the timing of the attack, which came as the political dispute between the KDP and the PUK intensified and Baghdad faced resistance from armed groups over its disarmament plans.

“The notable point about the timing of the targeting of the Khor Mor field is that it coincides with political disagreements between the KDP and the PUK, as well as the escalating disagreements between the Iraqi prime minister and some armed factions over handing their weapons to the state,” he said.

The Reuters news agency has reported that the attack originated from the Tuz Khurmatu area of Salah al-Din governorate, outside of northern Iraq’s semi-autonomous Kurdish region – although neither the launch location nor the perpetrators have been officially established so far. Al-Abed called on the Iraqi central government to identify those responsible and hold them accountable.

Al-Abed said the economic consequences of further attacks could extend beyond areas administered by the KRG, given the field’s role in electricity generation in the neighbouring governorates of Kirkuk and Nineveh.

“The Iraqi government must announce the identity of the parties seeking to destroy the country’s economy and hold them accountable,” he said. “The situation in Iraq could explode at any moment because some armed factions are not complying with the demand to hand over their weapons to the state. If war breaks out again between Iran and the US, these factions may intervene in the confrontation, and Iraq could then turn into a battlefield.”

Clare Lombardelli, the Bank’s deputy governor for monetary policy, said the unfolding conflict, which has triggered a surge in energy prices and clouded the outlook for the economy, was contributing to an increase in youth…
articles.body:
Young people in Britain are bearing the brunt of a “low-gear economy” as employers hold back from hiring amid the fallout from the war in the Middle East, a deputy governor of the Bank of England has warned.

Clare Lombardelli, the Bank’s deputy governor for monetary policy, said the unfolding conflict, which has triggered a surge in energy prices and clouded the outlook for the economy, was contributing to an increase in youth unemployment.

“What you see is the cost falling on young people, so you can see this rapid rise in the number of young people who are struggling to find jobs,” she said.

Against a highly volatile backdrop, she also warned Threadneedle Street was preparing for a “live” decision on interest rates next month after it increased the cost of borrowing last week for the first time in three years.

In an interview with the Guardian, Lombardelli said the UK’s employers were attempting to navigate the complex geopolitical backdrop by holding on to staff and freezing new recruitment.

“It’s what I call a low-gear economy. So a labour market where you’re seeing a real fall-off in hiring. But actually, we’re not seeing much in the way of redundancies. What’s going on is this kind of low hire, low fire dynamic,” she said.

“They [employers] are delaying hiring. They want to see if this uncertainty is going to resolve – like all of us. None of us thought we’d be nine months into this conflict.

“If firms are not hiring, obviously, by definition, that means people that are new to the labour market are hurt by that.”

Her comments come as Andy Burnham’s government awaits the findings of a report into young people and work by the former Labour cabinet minister, Alan Milburn, which is expected to be published next week.

With employers facing rising costs triggered by the Iran war, higher taxes and weaker levels of demand from consumers squeezed by the cost of living crisis, unemployment in the UK has risen this year to 4.7%. Youth unemployment has risen at a sharper rate to the highest levels outside the Covid pandemic since 2015.

Tackling the UK’s youth jobs crisis is also a growing priority for the government after an increase in the number of young people who are not in education, employment or training (Neet) to almost a million.

Lombardelli is expected to outline her concerns over a slowdown in labour market dynamism at a speech in London on Tuesday.

Lombardelli joined the majority of the Bank’s monetary policy committee (MPC) in voting to lift the base rate from 3.75% to 4%. She said a further quarter-point rise could be warranted from as early as its next policy meeting in December.

“Every meeting is live for us. December is, you know, it’s certainly plausible. What’s the market pricing at the moment? It’s about 50/50 for December,” she said.

“I think it depends what we see on the conflict and the energy prices and it depends what we see in the wider data and how all that fits together. But I wouldn’t rule it out. Equally, I don’t have enough information just yet.”

Lombardelli was among members of the MPC who joined the Bank’s governor, Andrew Bailey, in raising the prospect of another rate rise in the near future – with a resolution to the Iran conflict the key factor that will influence the decision.

Oil prices have fallen sharply, to below $100 a barrel, after the Democrats’ victories in the US Congress, which some investors have interpreted as potentially constraining Donald Trump’s capacity to prolong the conflict in Iran. Trump said at the weekend that he was highly unlikely to order fresh attacks on Iran as long as talks to end the conflict progressed.

Lombardelli, a former Treasury and OECD economist, said the impact of an increasingly stagnant jobs market was being seen particularly in sectors that offer young people their first job. “So that might be hospitality, it might be retail, in particular,” she said. “If you look at the distribution of where variances are, they’ve really fallen off in those sectors where young people can get their first start in the labour market.”

She added that employers surveyed by the Bank suggested there is “a sense that hiring a young person is a higher risk than it used to be”.

Threadneedle Street is focusing heavily on the jobs market amid concerns that current high levels of inflation could become entrenched in the economy if workers have enough bargaining power to push for higher wage settlements – which could lead companies to put up their prices to cover higher wage bills, stoking inflation. Signs of a weaker labour market could diminish this risk.

However, Lombardelli said that higher levels of unemployment would not necessarily bear down on inflationary pressures. This is because employers – holding on to the staff they needed – were only hiring for positions they found harder to fill.

“You can have higher unemployment without it exerting a downward pressure on inflation,” she said. “So that’s obviously a problem.”

articles.title: Israeli forces kill 14-year-old Palestinian boy in occupied West Bank

Israeli forces have shot and killed a 14-year-old Palestinian boy and wounded two other teens during a raid on the village of Burqa in the occupied West Bank, according to officials. The Palestinian Ministry of Health identified the victim on Tuesday as Moataz Iyad Daghlas and said Israeli authorities were withholding his body.
articles.body:
Israel’s military says its soldiers opened fire to prevent Palestinians from throwing stones at vehicles in Burqa.

Israeli forces have shot and killed a 14-year-old Palestinian boy and wounded two other teens during a raid on the village of Burqa in the occupied West Bank, according to officials.

The Palestinian Ministry of Health identified the victim on Tuesday as Moataz Iyad Daghlas and said Israeli authorities were withholding his body.

The Palestinian Wafa news agency reported that two other teenagers were wounded – a 17-year-old shot in the abdomen and pelvis and a 19-year-old hit in the hand.

The Israeli military confirmed the shooting in Burqa, which is located near the city of Nablus.

In a statement, the military said soldiers opened fire to prevent Palestinians from throwing stones at Israeli vehicles.

“The forces responded with gunfire to neutralise the threat and several hits were confirmed,” it said.

According to Wafa, soldiers detained Moataz’s father and stopped an ambulance from reaching the wounded.

They briefly held three volunteer paramedics from the Palestine Red Crescent Society who were working in the area, it reported.

The attacks come as Israeli pogroms in the occupied West Bank surge to what the United Nations has called an “unprecedented level”, following the Hamas-led attacks on southern Israel on October 7, 2023 and the subsequent genocidal war on Gaza.

According to the UN, at least 1,143 Palestinians have been killed in the occupied West Bank since October 7, 2023, including 250 children.

The figure includes Palestinians killed by Israeli settlers living in illegal settlements in the occupied West Bank.

The Armed Conflict Location & Event Data Project (ACLED) said 2026 is on track to be the most violent year for settler-related violence since it began monitoring the territory a decade ago. In July alone, 11 people were killed in four incidents involving armed settlers alongside Israeli forces.

Hebron, Ramallah, Nablus, Jenin, and el-Bireh have seen the worst of the settlers’ pogroms.

articles.title: US officials seek ‘final end’ to Russia-Ukraine war as Abu Dhabi talks begin
articles.summary: First substantive peace talks since February to include US proposal for ‘long-term security architecture’ between Moscow and Europe US officials said they would seek a “final end” to the war between Russia and Ukraine, beginning with trilateral talks in Abu Dhabi on Tuesday in the first substantive negotiations between the two countries since February. The talks are also the first since the US launched joint strikes with Israel against Iran, and they follow bruising midterm elections that have weakened Donald Trump at home. Continue reading...
articles.preview: First substantive peace talks since February to include US proposal for ‘long-term security architecture’ between Moscow and Europe US officials said they would seek a “final end” to the war between Russia and Ukraine, beginning with trilateral talks in Abu Dhabi on Tuesday in the first substantive negotiations between the two countries since February. The talks are also the first since the US launched joint strikes with Israel against Iran, and they follow bruising midterm elections that have weakened Donald Trump at home. Continue reading...
articles.body:
US officials said they would seek a “final end” to the war between Russia and Ukraine, beginning with trilateral talks in Abu Dhabi on Tuesday in the first substantive negotiations between the two countries since February.

The talks are also the first since the US launched joint strikes with Israel against Iran, and they follow bruising midterm elections that have weakened Donald Trump at home.

Part of the Trump administration’s proposal involves drawing a new “long-term security architecture” between Russia and Europe, administration officials have said.

European officials are concerned that Russia may stick to its hardline demands that Nato should roll back its military footprint across eastern Europe, which would threaten to leave allies vulnerable to Moscow’s influence at a time of historic tensions with the west.

Since his first decade in power, Vladimir Putin has complained about Nato’s eastward expansion and sought to renegotiate the balance of power between Nato and Russia – but never before have those demands been embraced by a sitting US administration, which has made it clear that it is desperate to get to a deal.

Previewing the discussions, a US administration official said the US would “need Europe at the table” to end the war. He said negotiators could also revive the Nato-Russian council that was suspended after Russia’s full-scale invasion in 2022, and potentially lift sanctions against Russia to get to a deal.

The US officials also claimed that they had discussed with Russia potential security guarantees to Ukraine similar to Nato’s article 5, which protect member states in case of an attack. Russia has strongly opposed Nato admitting Ukraine or western countries placing troops in Ukraine.

“What they would be getting would be effectively very similar to Nato,” an administration official said.

“Getting a US security guarantee is a really, really big deal,” the official added, saying it would be up to Donald Trump and Ukraine’s Volodymyr Zelenskyy to discuss. “And if he wants to do that, that’s that’s a very, very big deal in terms of resources and funding and military support.”

Critics have expressed skepticism about what may trigger those security guarantees, however, noting that article 5 does not oblige Nato member states to defend others, and that cyber-attacks and other forms of hybrid warfare have blurred the line for what would require a military response.

Jared Kushner, Trump’s son-in-law and a lead negotiator for the United States, described a potential new framework for European in general terms on Monday, saying the US would seek “stronger consultation, reliable crisis communications, greater military transparency, and reciprocal measures to reduce escalation risks, while fully respecting the sovereignty and independent decision-making of every nation”.

European delegations from Germany, France, the United Kingdom, Italy and the European Union will meet US negotiators in Abu Dhabi to discuss the “long-term security architecture between Russia and Europe in order to figure out how to reduce future conflicts”.

A European security official from a country attending the talks said that the US proposal was not yet clear and that they were bracing themselves for the US to pose serious concessions to Russia during the Abu Dhabi consultations.

“We already have a European security architecture in place,” said Kaja Kallas, the European Union’s top diplomat, at a G7 foreign ministers meeting on Monday. “This includes international agreements under which Russia has undertaken obligations, including with regard to sovereignty and territorial integrity. The problem is that Russia is not respecting these agreements.”

Donald Trump has also said that Ukraine would like be expected to give up territory in a final deal, and would end with a “little bit different shape“.

Trump last week after meeting with Kremlin advisor Kirill Dmitriev said he would seek a “big, beautiful agreement” that “might involve all of Europe”. Critics are concerned that Trump and Putin could try to go over the heads of European leaders in order to negotiate a peace that gives serious concessions to Russia.

“There’s a lot of baggage that people in Europe have about this idea,” said a US administration official, pointing specifically to Russia’s 2021 proposal that was viewed as an ultimatum to Nato to get out of eastern Europe.

In 2021, Russia issued a list of demands to Nato that included a ban on expansion to new countries including Ukraine, a rollback of troops to its pre-1997 borders, and limits on where it could place missiles. Nato rejected that proposal and Russia invaded Ukraine less than a month later.

“We have to build something new that works today… Because if all the old architecture was working well, then we wouldn’t be in this long war. And so obviously something’s not working, and we need to come up with a way that when we end this war, it really is a final end to the war,” said the US administration official.

The content of those proposals are not clear yet, although the secretary of state, Marco Rubio, claimed on Monday “there’s been some advances made in what that architecture should look”.

“We obviously have to get past the conflict to get to that point,” he added.
