articles.title: Fossil fuel emissions fall due to Iran war and renewables, research shows
articles.summary: The expected annual drop would be the first since 2020, when the COVID-19 pandemic paralyzed the global economy, trade and transport.
articles.preview: Antalya, Turkey – Global fossil fuel emissions are projected to fall slightly in 2026 due to the expansion of renewable energy and the oil price shock sparked by the Iran war, researchers said Tuesday. Emissions from the burning of oil, gas and coal — the main drivers of climate change — rose by 0.9% per year, on average, in the past decade, hitting a record high in 2025, according to the Global Carbon Budget report.
articles.body:
Antalya, Turkey – Global fossil fuel emissions are projected to fall slightly in 2026 due to the expansion of renewable energy and the oil price shock sparked by the Iran war, researchers said Tuesday.

Emissions from the burning of oil, gas and coal — the main drivers of climate change — rose by 0.9% per year, on average, in the past decade, hitting a record high in 2025, according to the Global Carbon Budget report.

But they are expected to drop by 0.4% in 2026, according to the research, published as nations meet at the U.N.’s COP31 climate summit in Antalya, Turkey.

It would be the first annual drop since 2020, when the COVID-19 pandemic paralyzed the global economy, trade and transport.

This year, the U.S.-led war in Iran and closure of the Strait of Hormuz played a role in driving emissions down as it caused a drop in oil consumption amid soaring crude prices, the researchers found.

The deployment of solar panels, wind farms and electric vehicles also contributed to the drop. Two thirds of the increase in global energy demand is being met by solar and wind power and electric vehicles, the report found.

“A decline in fossil CO2 emissions is encouraging, but a reduction driven partly by geopolitical shocks is not a sustainable climate solution,” said Pierre Friedlingstein, director of the Global Carbon Budget Office at the University of Exeter in Britain.

“The long-term answer remains the rapid deployment of clean energy technologies,” said Friedlingstein, who led the study published in the journal Earth System Science Data.

Corinne Le Quere, a climate change science professor at the University of East Anglia, noted that emissions rebounded when economies recovered following shocks such as COVID-19 or the global financial crisis.

A rebound is likely “when the oil tensions go away,“ she said in a media briefing.

Oil-related emissions are projected to drop 1.9% last year, but it was “likely a short-term response to the energy shock triggered by the Iran conflict,“ the researchers said.

Gas emissions are set to fall 0.3% while those from coal use will rise 0.6%.

Overall, fossil carbon dioxide emissions are expected to reach 38.2 billion metric tons in 2026.

Including emissions from land-use change such as deforestation, total CO2 emissions are projected to rise to 43.3 billion metric tons, from 42.8 billion metric tons last year.

The researchers said land-use emissions are projected to rise partly due to peat fires and forest degradation in southeast Asia, associated with drier conditions linked to this year’s exceptionally strong El Nino climate pattern.

The report found that the world’s carbon budget — the amount of CO2 that can be emitted before global warming exceeds 1.5 degrees Celsius above preindustrial levels — stands at 150 billion metric tons.

The researchers calculated that at the current, the carbon budget would be exhausted in less than four years.

Nations agreed at the 2015 U.N. climate talks in Paris to keep global warming “well below” 2C above preindustrial levels, while pursuing efforts to limit it to 1.5C.

But the United Nations declared in September that the long-term 1.5C target would be missed in a matter of years.

Scientists say it is crucial to reduce greenhouse gas emissions from fossil fuels to limit the period of “overshoot” above 1.5C and bring temperatures back down as quickly as possible.

articles.title: The superpower battle over energy – and what it means for your bills
articles.summary: A tug-of-war between China and the US could have a big impact on energy costs, but who will win?
articles.preview: A gas rig in the North Sea. An oil field in Texas. A solar panel factory in China. They can feel a world away, but your energy bill says otherwise. In January, it could jump by more than a quarter â around Â£460 extra a year for the typical UK household â according to the latest forecasts from the big suppliers British Gas, EDF and E.ON. For the second time in four years, a war thousands of miles away is landing in British inboxes. Since US and Israeli strikes on Iran in February effectively closed the Strait of Hormuz, oil and gas prices have soared.
articles.body:
A gas rig in the North Sea. An oil field in Texas. A solar panel factory in China. They can feel a world away, but your energy bill says otherwise.

In January, it could jump by more than a quarter â around Â£460 extra a year for the typical UK household â according to the latest forecasts from the big suppliers British Gas, EDF and E.ON.

For the second time in four years, a war thousands of miles away is landing in British inboxes.

Since US and Israeli strikes on Iran in February effectively closed the Strait of Hormuz, oil and gas prices have soared.

Winter is expected to push them higher still: demand for gas is rising just as Europe's winter gas stores are at their lowest since records began in 2011.

And there's a bigger threat looming over all of this: the warming climate. Cutting carbon emissions is essential to limit future warming and avoid the most damaging effects of climate change. But keeping bills down while cutting emissions is proving hard â and not just for the UK.

As world leaders gather this week in Antalya, Turkey, for COP31, the UN climate summit, the same tension is playing out around the world. Energy and climate policy has become the front line in a contest between the world's two energy superpowers, leaving everyone else squeezed in between.

America is betting on fossil-fuel molecules: pumping record volumes of oil and gas and pressing its allies to buy them. China is betting on electrons: flooding the world with the solar panels, batteries and electric cars that can replace those fuels.

Whether the bet on fossil fuels or renewables wins will shape not just what the world pays for energy, but how fast it can cut the emissions that are heating the planet.

The UK, which already buys nearly a quarter of its imported gas from America and much of its clean energy kit from China, is being pulled both ways. So which path will it take? Is there a middle way and what will it all mean for your bills?

Two decisions

On the Moray Firth near Inverness, a long spit of sand and dunes curls out into the sea at Whiteness Head. Behind it lies a yard where, for nearly 30 years, thousands of workers built the giant platforms that opened up North Sea oil.

Ming Yang, one of China's biggest wind turbine makers, wanted to bring it back to life with a £1.5bn factory and up to 1,500 jobs initially generated. In March, after US lawmakers had urged the UK to block it, ministers did just that, citing national security.

Last month, they approved a new North Sea gas field, Jackdaw. No to Chinese wind turbines; yes to North Sea gas.

Few countries are more exposed to the energy shock than the UK. Gas heats most homes and, much of the time, sets the wholesale price of electricity. The last shock, after Russia's invasion of Ukraine, cost households an extra Â£63bn â around Â£2,200 each â according to the Energy and Climate Intelligence Unit and E3G, two climate and energy research organisations.

Less than half of the UK's gas now comes from its own North Sea fields, and the energy we import often comes from places that turn out to be unstable or unreliable.

At the same time, Energy Secretary Miatta Fahnbulleh says tackling climate change remains a priority after Britain's hottest summer on record. The heatwaves, droughts and wildfires it brought would have been almost impossible without global warming, the Met Office's chief scientist told BBC Panorama.

But when I pressed Fahnbulleh on which matters most, bills or climate, she was unequivocal: "With the cost of living biting, affordability is my overriding objective, without a doubt."

"We are far too exposed to global markets we have no control over," Fahnbulleh told me. "What's the solution to that? Homegrown clean energy."

There are two ways to make Britain's energy more homegrown: drill for more of it, or build more of it.

The case for drilling

Within hours of Jackdaw's approval, US President Donald Trump - at war with wind turbines since objecting to a wind farm near his Aberdeenshire golf course in 2006 - took to Truth Social. "They should go FULL BLAST!!!" he wrote. "TAKE DOWN THE COSTLY AND RIDICULOUS WINDMILLS!"

Now the UK government faces a tougher choice - whether to approve Rosebank, west of Shetland, the UK's largest undeveloped oil field.

Rosebank is far bigger than Jackdaw - Fahnbulleh has said it would produce about seven times the emissions - and it is mostly oil, not gas. The subject has reportedly split the cabinet. A decision is expected within weeks.

The government's opponents are already blaming high bills on its reluctance to drill. Conservative leader Kemi Badenoch has told the prime minister to "stop faffing about" and give permission, calling drilling "the only way we can protect families from rising bills".

"If we use our own gasâ¦ that will bring our bills down," says Reform UK's Richard Tice.

Last week's US midterms were a reminder of the political risks. Soaring petrol prices are widely seen as a key reason Trump's Republicans lost control of Congress.

But when I asked Fahnbulleh whether producing more British oil and gas would bring bills down, she was clear. "No, it doesn't," she said. "In the end, the oil and gas is sold on global markets."

Critics go further. Rosebank "doesn't really do anything for energy security", argues Tessa Khan of the campaign group Uplift, which has fought the field in the courts. "What it does do is send a very dangerous signal about the UK's seriousness about addressing climate change after the summer that we've just had."

Zoom out, though, and the row looks rather different. The North Sea is in long-term decline. Output has fallen by more than two-thirds since its peak in 1999, and the Office for Budget Responsibility expects it to keep falling by around 10% a year â even with Rosebank, which its forecast assumes goes ahead.

Whatever ministers decide, the basin's most productive days are behind it. Jackdaw's reserves amount to only a few months of UK gas demand, while Rosebank contains less than a year's worth of our oil consumption.

And last week the government introduced a bill to write its ban on new exploration licences into law. Rosebank, which is already licensed, is not covered. That could let ministers have it both ways: approve the last big field, while promising there will never be another.

With bills set to rise again in January, that may prove a tempting combination.

The case for electrons

The alternative is to build.

Gas is bought, burned and bought again. A wind turbine or solar panel costs money to put up but can then generate electricity for decades without needing shipments of fuel.

The government's climate advisers, the Climate Change Committee, calculate that a future price shock like 2022's would push household energy bills up 59% if Britain stayed on a high-carbon path - but only 4% if it focused on renewables.

The cost of power from new solar farms fell by 90% between 2010 and 2024, and from onshore wind by 70%, according to the International Renewable Energy Agency. But the recent bout of global inflation has been pushing initial costs back up. Last year the Danish developer Ãrsted scrapped plans for Hornsea 4, a giant wind farm off the Yorkshire coast, blaming soaring supply chain costs.

Higher interest rates have made things worse. Most of the cost of a wind or solar farm comes up front, so developers must borrow heavily before they generate any power.

And there is another problem. Britain needs expensive new electricity networks to bring that renewable power to the towns and cities where it is needed. Meanwhile, gas-fired stations still frequently set wholesale power prices - meaning any cost savings are not always reflected in customer bills.

All of which means building more renewables does not automatically mean lower household bills.

The China question

And there is another issue - China's dominance of clean tech. It makes the vast majority of the world's solar panels and batteries, and around two-thirds of its electric cars.

And China's lead is growing. In March, its exports of solar panels, batteries and electric cars hit a record, up 70% on a year earlier, according to the think tank Ember.

The UK wants to escape the fossil fuels that leave households exposed to price shocks and keep adding to global warming. Much of the technology needed to replace those fuels comes from China - a country it is increasingly reluctant to depend on.

I asked Fahnbulleh whether Britain was swapping dependence on petrostates for dependence on Beijing. "Well, look, we are," she said, adding: "we've got a diversified global market".

Britain will keep buying from China where it needs to, says Fahnbulleh, but she wants more of the kit made here. "I want to see turbines," she said.

Yet UK-built turbines were exactly what Ming Yang was offering.

"There was a security risk, and national security comes first and foremost," says Fahnbulleh. The government has never publicly explained what that risk was.

Two days before Jackdaw was approved, Japan's Sumitomo Electric opened Britain's first HVDC subsea cable factory at Nigg, a short way up the coast from Whiteness Head, creating up to 250 jobs.

Foreign investment, then - just not from China.

Role reversal

Earlier this year the US formally left the Paris climate agreement and is not expected to send a delegation to this year's COP. Without American pressure, others have less reason to make bold promises: national pledges now add up to a cut in global emissions of just 6% by 2035, the UN says â a tenth of what scientists say is needed to limit warming to 1.5C.

China is beginning to fill the space. Li Shuo, of the Asia Society Policy Institute, calls it a "role reversal". Once "a very conservative player" at climate talks, China now sees pushing the global climate agenda as serving its national interest â and, he says, "we're only at the beginning of this". It aims to hit one of COP31's flagship goals, getting 35% of its energy from electricity, five years early.

And increasingly it is Chinese companies, rather than governments' promises, that are driving the transition. "It's really just a China story," says Li Shuo.

If that is right, it leaves the UK in an uncomfortable place. Hard choices â and they come when household budgets are already stretched thin.

articles.body:
Ukraine, Russia and US return to talks in Abu Dhabi: What to expect?

November 10, 2026

Ukrainian and Russian representatives last met in February for talks on ending the war, but the same sticking points remain. Ukraine continues to demand security guarantees, which is a non-starter for Russia.

A new round of trilateral talks between Russia, Ukraineand the United States are scheduled to take place in Abu Dhabi on Tuesday and Wednesday, months after a flurry of US-mediated peace talks earlier this year in January and February went nowhere.

When announcing the new trilateral talks last week, US special envoy Steve Witkoff said the discussions would focus on "post-war security arrangements, de-escalation, humanitarian efforts, and next steps toward peace."

Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy has named security guarantees, an energy ceasefire, unblocking the Black Sea, extended prisoner exchanges, and preparations for a meeting of the leaders of Ukraine, the United States and Russia as his key topics.

Lawmaker Davyd Arakhamia, a member of Ukraine's delegation, told DW he was not expecting quick progress.

"I don't think there will be a breakthrough, after there was such a long break in the negotiation process," he said. "Simply the fact that trilateral talks are being resumed can be counted as a success."

Who is sitting at the table?

Witkoff will be joined by US President Donald Trump's son-in-law, real estate developer Jared Kushner, who serves as special envoy.

The Kremlin has sent Vladimir Medinsky, an aide to Russian President Vladimir Putin, to act as chief negotiator, along with a delegation including high-ranking Russian military and intelligence officials.

The Ukrainian delegation will be led by Rustem Umerov, head of Ukraine's Foreign Intelligence Service, along with Arakhamia, and diplomatic and military officials.

Europe joins in

Separate formats are planned with several European representatives.

These include Günter Sautter, German Chancellor Friedrich Merz's foreign and security policy adviser, Emmanuel Bonne, head of the Elysee Palace's diplomatic service and Jonathan Powell, the UK's national security advisor, and Fabrizio Saggio, diplomatic adviser to Italian Prime Minister Giorgia Meloni.

Björn Seibert, Chief of Staff for the President of the European Commission, Ursula von der Leyen, and Geoffrey van Leeuwen, Chief of Staff for NATO Secretary-General Mark Rutte, will also attend.

It's doubtful, however, whether European representatives will be formally involved in talks on a potential peace deal.

Hanna Shelest, a security studies director at the foreign policy network Ukrainian Prism, told DW she believed they'd play "an observing role, at best."

She added that, until now, Russia had been reluctant to have European representatives at the table to uphold the impression that talks were "a matter between two superpowers" — namely, Russia and the United States — and to increase pressure on Washington.

"I doubt the Russian delegation will let the Europeans have a say," she told DW.

"Experience from the past years has taught us that as soon as Medinsky heads negotiations, the point becomes demonstrating to the US that Russia is willing to talk, but in reality, they won't reach an agreement," she explained. "Instead, there will be a long sermon about history and all sorts of other things."

However, she said Moscow sending high-ranking intelligence officers as part of the delegation was a "fairly positive aspect" of Russia's intentions.

She believed that additional negotiations were possible at this level.

This could include over prisoner exchanges or humanitarian pauses in villages near Oleshky, a town in the Russian occupied Kherson region in Ukraine's south, where US First Lady Melania Trump was credited with arranging a temporary truce in late October that secured humanitarian aid and allowed civilians to evacuate.

But despite these "positive signals," Shelest cautioned against hoping for concrete results, and suspected Russia was using the talks to stall.

Oleshky truce as a template for wider ceasefire?

Late last week, Trump spoke of a "big beautiful agreement," after speaking with Russian envoy Kirill Dmitriev, "that might involve all of Europe."

This new security architecture, Kushner later clarified on social media, would be centered around "permanent security consultations, reliable crisis communications, greater military transparency, reciprocal measures to reduce escalation risks, and an enduring framework for long-term European security and stability."

These points "don't contain anything the Russians haven't been talking about since 2009," Shelest said.

Ivan Us, chief consultant and economic diplomacy expert at Ukraine's National Institute for Strategic Studies, pointed out that negotiations with people who are not decisions-makers could be simply for show.

But he agreed with other expert observers that negotiators in Abu Dhabi might try to use the temporary truce brokered for Oleshky as a model for other limited humanitarian ceasefires in the region.

But while Us said he saw cause for optimism, he also cautioned that Russia had continued attacks in Ukraine during the Oleshky truce, and had used the pause to fortify its positions around the town.

This article was originally published in Ukrainian.

articles.body:
Il Congresso americano ha riaperto i battenti in uno scenario politico profondamente cambiato dopo la dura sconfitta inflitta dai democratici ai repubblicani nelle elezioni di metà mandato e la resa dei conti è già iniziata. Il deputato repubblicano Thomas Massie ha presentato alla Camera la mozione per l'impeachment contro Pete Hegseth, principale bersaglio del dopo midterm assieme ad Elon Musk.

Ma Donald Trump continua a difendere Pete Hegseth. "Ha vinto due guerre, in Iran e Venezuela", ha detto in una conferenza stampa alla Casa Bianca definendo il senatore repubblicano Thomas Massie, che ha proposto l'impeachment "uno sfigato"

Gli otto articoli presentati dal repubblicano del Kentucky, uno dei piu' critici verso Donald Trump, accusano il segretario alla Difesa di "gravi reati e illeciti", tra cui l'aver avviato senza l'autorizzazione del Congresso una guerra contro l'Iran e l'aver causato la morte di centinaia di civili nel corso di attacchi condotti via mare contro presunti trafficanti di droga nei Caraibi. Hegseth è anche accusato di ritorsione nei confronti del senatore democratico Mark Kelly e di sequestro di persona dell'ex leader venezuelano Nicolás Maduro nell'operazione 'Absolute Resolve''. La mozione potrebbe essere votata già entro questa settimana. Fonti interne sia repubblicane che democratiche indicano che esiste una reale possibilità che l'impeachment contro il capo del Pentagono venga approvato alla Camera, dove basta una maggioranza semplice.

Tra i primi repubblicani a commentare il segretario di stato Marco Rubio: "La procedura di impeachment contro Hegseth è ingiusta, è un grande professionista", ha detto a margine del G7 di Parigi.

Il leader dei dem, Hakeem Jeffries, si è dichiarato "assolutamente favorevole" alla risoluzione, mentre molti repubblicani sono furiosi con Hegseth, ritenuto responsabile della pesante sconfitta del partito alle elezioni. Anche in caso di approvazione alla House, per la destituzione formale di Hegseth ci vorrebbe un processo e una maggioranza dei due terzi al Senato. Al momento è considerato uno scenario molto improbabile. Potrebbe anche darsi però che Trump siluri il suo segretario alla Difesa prima di arrivare all'impeachment. Fino ad oggi ha continuato a difenderlo pubblicamente ma il tycoon non è nuovo a improvvise giravolte nei confronti dei suoi alleati e consiglieri. Hegseth ribadisce di non essere preoccupato e che se tornasse indietro rifarebbe tutto come prima con la guerra all'Iran. "Una decisione non deve necessariamente essere popolare per essere necessaria", ha dichiarato aggiungendo che Trump "ha il controllo della situazione, qualunque strada decida di intraprendere". "Non potrei essere più orgoglioso di ciò che il nostro presidente ha realizzato, delle decisioni che ha preso, delle scelte coraggiose che ha compiuto, dell'audacia dei nostri vertici militari e della competenza e del coraggio dei soldati sul campo. Pertanto, se qualcuno vuole contestare operazioni come 'Epic Fury', 'Rough Rider' o la cattura di Nicolás Maduro, sta contestando le truppe e i risultati che hanno ottenuto", ha affermato, il capo del Pentagono.

Nel frattempo il presidente ha continuato a mettere in dubbio la correttezza del voto. "Qualcuno crede davvero che questa 'elezione' sia stata onesta? Come hanno potuto i sondaggi sbagliare così tanto?", ha scritto il presidente su Truth. Il commander-in-chief ha anche parlato dei suoi nemici sostenendo che non li perdonerà mai anche se questo dovesse costargli "il paradiso". "La risposta più facile sarebbe sì, li posso perdonare", ha detto Trump al giornalista di Cbs che gli aveva rivolto la domanda citando in particolare l'ex speaker della Camera Nancy Pelosi e l'ex direttore dell'Fbi James Comey. "Ma non sarei onesto", ha poi aggiunto. "Odio davvero alcuni dei miei nemici. Individui estremamente disonesti, persone pessime, molto dannose per il nostro Paese. Amo il nostro Paese molto più di quanto possa amare delle persone, specialmente persone del genere".

articles.title: The French fridge hacks were relatively unsophisticated. An AI-enabled attack would raise the stakes

articles.body:
Iranian hackers like to send a message.

In 2023 a state-backed group interrupted TV streaming services in the United Arab Emirates to broadcast a deepfake report on the war in Gaza. In the same year, hackers affiliated with Iran displayed the slogan “down with Israel” on the screens of water-control equipment made by an Israeli firm.

Now France has attributed an attack on supermarket fridges to hackers operating under the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps, a key branch of Iran’s military establishment.

There was no message this time, but the disruption made headlines around the world. Some refrigerators had their temperature turned up so high they caught fire. In the hours after the hack, supermarket employees dumped piles of perished meat and melted ice-cream into rubbish containers.

France’s foreign minister described it as an act of “unprecedented scale and unprecedented aggression” and promised “Europe-wide sanctions” would be imposed against those responsible.

It follows attacks on industrial freezers at an Israeli food production plant in May and a wave of freezer malfunctions that spoiled food at US military bases in August that are now reportedly being treated as a suspected hack. Those attacks have not been officially attributed to Iran, but the French announcement is the first to implicate the state in this type of hack.

Rafe Pilling, a senior director at Sophos, a cybersecurity firm, said the relatively unsophisticated nature of the attack – hackers used default passwords to access fridge controls – was in line with Iranian capabilities. “The attacks themselves were not particularly complex,” he said.

Pilling said there was now a presumption the French attacks and a wave of rogue defrosting hacks across Europe last week were linked.

Hostile cyber operations against the west tend to come from a vexatious quartet of China, Russia, Iran and North Korea. All have different aims and characteristics: China has focused on industrial espionage and mass data gathering, Russia on disrupting enemy infrastructure and spreading disinformation, and North Korea on hacking crypto exchanges because it needs money. Iran, according to Pilling, wants to put a shot across the bow of its enemies.

“In general Iran uses cyber-attacks to project power internationally and to signal their political displeasure with regional and international adversaries,” Pilling said.

The fridge hacks came as the UK’s national cybersecurity centre warned the country is in the “foothills” of a new level of cyber threat – and should expect a “huge rise” in the volume of incidents. The main concern is AI, a technology now capable of highlighting previously unforeseen flaws in IT systems and helping attackers plan and carry out attacks.

However, the underlying context of the fridge attacks is not AI but geopolitics. After all, the refrigeration system vulnerabilities were relatively easy to find and exploit. But a combination of groundbreaking technology and tense global relations makes for an alarming landscape.

articles.body:
Kenya

Kenyan police have confiscated 454 kilograms of methamphetamine valued at $27 million in a joint operation with Tanzanian authorities targeting cross-border drug trafficking.

The drugs were discovered in Msambweni, on Kenya's coast, following investigations that began with the arrest of a suspect in Tanzania last week.

According to police, the suspect was transferred to Kenya and helped investigators locate the consignment. The individual was also allegedly connected to an earlier seizure of 250 kilograms of suspected methamphetamine and cocaine in Tanzania.

Three other suspects, including two Tanzanians and a Ugandan, were arrested during the operation. All four remain in police custody pending court appearances.

Officers also confiscated two vehicles and a motorcycle believed to be linked to the operation.

The seizure comes amid growing concern over drug trafficking along East Africa's coastline.

Last month, Kenyan authorities destroyed more than a tonne of methamphetamine intercepted by the country's navy off the coast of Mombasa last year.

Kenya's Deputy President Kithure Kindiki has identified illegal drugs and alcohol abuse as major national threats, pledging tougher legislation and increased enforcement.

The Institute for Security Studies has warned that East Africa is increasingly becoming both a transit corridor for international drug shipments and a destination for illicit substances.

Police say investigations into the latest seizure are continuing.

articles.title: Che cosa ha deciso la Corte costituzionale su Giusi Bartolozzi
articles.summary: È stato accolto solo in parte il conflitto di attribuzione sollevato dalla Camera, e ora l’ex capa di gabinetto di Nordio potrà essere processata per false dichiarazioni
articles.preview: Che cosa succede adesso La decisione ha conseguenze diverse per le due questioni esaminate. Per quanto riguarda l’eventuale concorso nei reati ministeriali, ora il Tribunale dei ministri dovrà esplicitare le ragioni per cui non lo ha configurato e la Procura dovrà comunicarle alla Camera. Quest’ultima potrà contestare la valutazione dei magistrati attraverso un nuovo conflitto di attribuzione, qualora ritenga che la mancata configurazione del concorso abbia indebitamente sottratto Bartolozzi alla procedura prevista per i reati ministeriali.
articles.body:
Che cosa succede adesso

La decisione ha conseguenze diverse per le due questioni esaminate. Per quanto riguarda l’eventuale concorso nei reati ministeriali, ora il Tribunale dei ministri dovrà esplicitare le ragioni per cui non lo ha configurato e la Procura dovrà comunicarle alla Camera. Quest’ultima potrà contestare la valutazione dei magistrati attraverso un nuovo conflitto di attribuzione, qualora ritenga che la mancata configurazione del concorso abbia indebitamente sottratto Bartolozzi alla procedura prevista per i reati ministeriali. In quel caso, la Corte costituzionale dovrebbe verificare se la valutazione dei magistrati abbia leso le prerogative della Camera, non accertare la responsabilità penale di Bartolozzi.

Quanto alle presunte false informazioni, il procedimento prosegue secondo le regole ordinarie, senza necessità di autorizzazione parlamentare. La Procura ha già emesso un decreto di citazione diretta a giudizio nei confronti di Bartolozzi, che quindi potrà andare a processo.

Resta da chiarire se Bartolozzi avrebbe dovuto essere ascoltata come indagata, anziché come persona informata sui fatti. In quest’ultimo caso era tenuta a dire la verità, ed è proprio dalle dichiarazioni rese in questa veste che è nata l’accusa di false informazioni. Se fosse stata ascoltata come indagata, avrebbe invece avuto il diritto di non rispondere. La Corte costituzionale ha lasciato aperta la questione delle eventuali conseguenze sui suoi diritti di difesa. La procura prospetta, dal canto suo, un’altra eventualità: se nel corso del giudizio per false informazioni dovessero emergere indizi di concorso nei reati attribuiti a Nordio, il giudice dovrebbe assolvere Bartolozzi e restituire gli atti al pubblico ministero, per avviare la procedura prevista per i reati ministeriali. Anche su questo profilo la Corte non si è pronunciata.

articles.title: Australia tightens AI oversight rules after OpenAI government breach
articles.summary: The decision comes after ​an OpenAI agent breached ​an Australian government website in June.
articles.preview: The decision comes after an OpenAI agent breached an Australian government website in June. Australia will make it mandatory for artificial intelligence companies to immediately report when their AI models go rogue and to open their models for evaluation, the government said. Prime Minister Anthony Albanese said on Tuesday the government had accepted all recommendations from a rapid review into the breach, which “include mandatory AI company reporting when it comes to misaligned behaviour or cyber-incidents, and consideration of reforming criminal law…
articles.body:
The decision comes after an OpenAI agent breached an Australian government website in June.

Australia will make it mandatory for artificial intelligence companies to immediately report when their AI models go rogue and to open their models for evaluation, the government said.

Prime Minister Anthony Albanese said on Tuesday the government had accepted all recommendations from a rapid review into the breach, which “include mandatory AI company reporting when it comes to misaligned behaviour or cyber-incidents, and consideration of reforming criminal law in cases of serious misconduct”.

“Australia is the first mover in this space, and we want to make sure that we continue to work so that we can reap the potential benefits from AI,” he said.

The decision comes after OpenAI-powered models hacked into an Australian government health data system in June, slipping past its digital defences and accessing files without authorisation.

Top AI firms have recently raised the alarm regarding the risk of humans losing control of their systems, calling for AI development to slow down to a pace that allows it to be safely regulated.

Earlier this year, Anthropic’s safety research scientist Evan Hubinger went so far as to say he believes there is a greater than 10 percent chance that AI could “kill all humans” within a decade.

Rapid incident notifications

The new Australian AI regulator will oversee security controls throughout the development and deployment of AI systems, identify and manage serious risks, and conduct independent evaluations of AI models.

The AI standards would also mandate rapid notification to the government of incidents such as “misaligned behaviour” conflicting with developers’ intentions.

Australian government documents define frontier AI as the most sophisticated models at the cutting edge of current technological capability.

Albanese told OpenAI chief executive Sam Altman that the US company took too long to inform the government of the incident. OpenAI apologised for the breach and its slow response.

Inquiry recommends law changes

A government inquiry into the June breach made several recommendations, including that the government consider changing the law.

The proposed AI regulator would follow Australia’s appointment of an eSafety Commissioner in 2015. The office describes itself as the world’s first government agency dedicated to keeping people safer online.

Since December last year, the commissioner has been enforcing a world-first ban on Australian children younger than 16 holding accounts on popular social media platforms.

articles.body:
OpenAI will not face criminal penalties over the Medicare data breach, but the prime minister has flagged changes to Australia’s criminal law to crack down on future breaches by artificial intelligence companies.

Anthony Albanese on Tuesday released the recommendations of a “rapid review” into the June breach of a Medicare statistics reporting service portal administered by Services Australia, but not the findings or the report itself, which he committed to releasing in the future.

A key recommendation is for the Attorney-General’s Department, the Australian federal police and home affairs to consider introducing “penalties for egregious regulatory non-compliance” and a “failure to prevent” offence, which would criminalise developing an AI model that engaged in harmful conduct while failing “to take reasonable steps to prevent that harm”.

The rapid review came in response to an AI agent, developed by OpenAI, accessing data from Services Australia and three other systems in June. The company did not notify the Australian government until mid-September despite becoming aware of the incident itself in August, prompting criticism from Labor and Albanese.

Guardian Australia revealed last month OpenAI used AI to help write the email to notify Australian authorities.

Sign up for Guardian Australia’s Politics, really newsletter here

Albanese said the government would set up a new AI safety regulator and implement six key obligations on AI companies:

- Maintaining security controls across all stages of development and deployment.

- Identifying and managing serious risks associated with their models.

- Providing mandatory notification of incidents to the Australian government rapidly.

- Allowing independent evaluation of their models.

- Maintaining and publishing safety and security frameworks to ensure good governance, risk management and transparency.

- Responding to updated standards and rules as technologies change.

The review recommended the federal government “consider mandatory, time-bound AI safety reporting”, including around AI agents behaving in ways their creators may not have intended.

The home affairs minister, Tony Burke, appearing with Albanese, told reporters: “It should never be the case that there’s an argument that someone didn’t know the computer was loaded.”

“We need to make sure that our laws and our systems keep pace with the technology and also make sure that we’re able to use the technology to find vulnerabilities before others do,” Burke said.

“The mandatory reporting, when artificial intelligence goes rogue, gives us a chance to be able to make sure that when this happens, the reporting occurs and occurs immediately.”

Despite the government’s earlier public anger at OpenAI, Albanese on Tuesday characterised the company’s breach of Services Australia as “minor” in terms of the implications for personal privacy. Guardian Australia understands OpenAI is unlikely to face further legal proceedings related to the June breach.

While Albanese did not directly answer a question about whether the OpenAI incident in June would have breached the proposed new laws if they were in place, government sources indicated that the new legislation would address similar future incidents.

“The clear indication is that no information was got that involves people’s personal details,” Albanese said.

“All of that was confirmed essentially … but that doesn’t mean that it wasn’t a serious issue and that in other areas there might be more serious implications.”

In a statement, an OpenAI spokesperson said the company was reviewing the recommendations and the government’s proposals.

“We have been in close dialogue with the government and we’ll continue to engage constructively as it develops its proposed legislation,” they said.

A separate OpenAI-led process, which is discussing better coordination between AI developers and the government, is expected to report back by 31 December.

The rapid review made 18 recommendations. Albanese said “we accept all of the recommendations and we’ve commenced work to implement them”.

The AI researcher Toby Walsh said the people in charge of AI companies needed to be criminally liable.

“We’ve tried fining them and we’re not the only ones. These companies are incredibly wealthy and it’s almost impossible to fine them enough,” Walsh said.

The Greens leader, David Shoebridge, branded Tuesday’s announcement a “capitulation” to the AI industry, claiming the reforms would not do enough to change behaviour. He said the government should have committed to implementing stronger changes rather than the recommendation to “consider” them.

“Safety keeps coming second to corporate investment, and this review locks that priority in by tying every AI safety effort to bringing in more AI money and more datacentres,” Shoebridge claimed.

“Being a world leader in AI doesn’t mean being a doormat to big tech. It means being prepared to regulate it, to protect Australians and to make sure corporate profits don’t come at the expense of everyone else.”

The shadow home affairs minister, Jonno Duniam, said the Coalition backed the announcement. He said “AI is too important to become an unnecessarily partisan political contest”, signalling an “enduring and multi-partisan approach” to the technology.

articles.title: Amid questions over Japan’s cybersecurity, just how safe is the My Number system?
articles.summary: With over 80% of the population using My Number, concerns have emerged over the country's all-in-one card and the personal information stored in it.
articles.preview: With companies reporting new data breaches almost daily in recent weeks — exposing millions of customers’ personal records in some cases — concerns are growing over whether it is only a matter of time before information held under Japan’s My Number system is compromised. The system uses a 12-digit number as a digital ID for residents, while the My Number card provides access to a range of government services involving highly sensitive personal information, including tax, pensions, medical history and family registry records.
articles.body:
With companies reporting new data breaches almost daily in recent weeks — exposing millions of customers’ personal records in some cases — concerns are growing over whether it is only a matter of time before information held under Japan’s My Number system is compromised.

The system uses a 12-digit number as a digital ID for residents, while the My Number card provides access to a range of government services involving highly sensitive personal information, including tax, pensions, medical history and family registry records.

The Digital Agency maintains that the system is secure because data is decentralized and stored across multiple locations, including local governments and businesses. This, it says, prevents attackers from gaining access to a broad range of personal information in a single breach, as might be possible in a centralized system. The system also complies with an internationally recognized security standard.

articles.title: Australia considers criminal penalties for rogue AI in wake of OpenAI hack
articles.summary: AI safety regulator will also be created after a rogue OpenAI agent hacked government websites.
articles.preview: Australia plans to create a new AI safety regulator and has flagged criminal penalties for tech companies who do not comply, months after an OpenAI hack. In September, Australia's Prime Minister Anthony Albanese revealed that a rogue OpenAI agent had "infiltrated" a government health website and other systems, and criticised the company for taking months to tell them about the hack.
articles.body:
Australia plans to create a new AI safety regulator and has flagged criminal penalties for tech companies who do not comply, months after an OpenAI hack.

In September, Australia's Prime Minister Anthony Albanese revealed that a rogue OpenAI agent had "infiltrated" a government health website and other systems, and criticised the company for taking months to tell them about the hack.

On Tuesday, he released the 18 recommendations made after a "rapid review" into the breaches including new safety and security standards for AI companies such as mandatory reporting of hacks.

AI brings opportunities, he said, but Australia must prepare for the "new risks" from this "rapidly advancing technology".

"The law needs to get ahead of and, in some cases, make sure that it catches up with, what is a very fast changing world," Albanese said.

One of the recommendations suggests changes to criminal law to have a standalone "failure to prevent" offence .

This would criminalise instances where a company develops "an AI model that engages in harmful conduct" and "fails to take reasonable steps to prevent that harm".

The review also recommended "mandatory, time-bound AI safety reporting" of hacks.

This point addresses what Albanese had earlier called his "disappointment" in the months-long delay for OpenAI to tell his government about the breach.

In June, a statistics portal containing "non-sensitive" data from Australia's universal healthcare scheme Medicare was hacked by a rogue OpenAI agent.

OpenAI said it only learnt of the breach in August while reviewing "misaligned model activity" and emailed a general inbox of an Australian government agency on 10 September.

It took several more days before the email was escalated to Australia's cybersecurity centre, with a message then sent to a government minister ahead of the prime minister being told.

Albanese said he spoke to OpenAI boss Sam Altman and raised "Australia's extreme concern about this incident", with Altman acknowledging there were "issues with protocols" at OpenAI.

Days after the hacks were revealed, OpenAI delayed its rollout of a new AI model, citing safety concerns.

Jensen Huang, the CEO and co-founder of the world’s most prominent chip company, has allegedly been honey-trapped by a suspected Chinese spy, and the news has struck the internet like a match to gasoline.

Huang has long been seen as a wife guy (or so everyone assumed). He and his wife, Lori, have been together since the 1980s, and both of their children work at Nvidia. Huang has been the closest thing the tech world has to a rock star, with fans lining up for selfies and autographs. Of all the AI overlords, the leather-jacket wearing Huang has seemed like the most level-headed and least erratic, which is why this plot twist has hit so hard.

The potential fallout is mind-boggling. Nvidia looms so large over the U.S. stock market that even the company’s domestic drama is a market risk. Countless AI startups depend on Nvidia chips, so any shake-up at the top would ripple far beyond the company. And Nvidia has no publicly disclosed succession plan, so if Huang leaves, it’s unclear who’d take over.

Is this how the AI bubble bursts? It’s a question that will be answered in time, but in the meantime, a more pressing matter demands our attention: ranking the funniest memes about the scandal, with bonus points for AI images presumably generated using Nvidia chips.

There’s admittedly a lot to choose from, ranging from “500 Days of Summer” jokes to jokes about divorce lawyers to an AI-adaptation of the music video for Usher‘s song “Confessions Pt. II,” a track about cheating. Another person created a viral AI video that recreates the Coldplay concert where a startup CEO was caught on the Jumbotron hugging a colleague.

Huang publicly confessed to the affair just yesterday, so the internet has the rest of the week to get creative.

Yes, the internet is having a field day with this one.

As usual, AI-generated content is doing a lot of heavy lifting. Copyleaks, a software company that analyzes online content for signs of AI and digital manipulation, said Monday that it had seen “an explosion in AI-manipulated photos and videos of Huang and Alice Huang, ranging from memes to more subtle edits.” The tally includes at least 70 AI-related posts on X, which together drew around 8.42 million views and 64,362 engagements as of Monday morning. Those metrics have almost certainly climbed since.

articles.body:
It’s difficult to overstate Nvidia’s power in today’s AI landscape. The company’s chips are the bedrock upon which advanced AI technology in the US is being built, and demand has consistently outpaced supply for years. Nvidia has also been an influential investor in a wide range of up-and-coming AI companies in recent years, with about $99 billion worth of equity investments in frontier AI labs, neoclouds, infrastructure companies, and more. Its chief executive has even become close with President Donald Trump.

The Nvidia CEO has been in a unique position to to influence AI export controls.

This is why, as both cofounder and longtime CEO of Nvidia, Jensen Huang would be a valuable target for a foreign adversary with sights on the American AI industry.

Huang is in hot water after news broke of his extramarital affair with an alleged Chinese spy, Alice Huang (no relation to Jensen) is an executive at Megaspeed, a Singapore-based cloud provider and a top Nvidia customer. Questions are swirling around how the affair may have influenced Huang’s reported push to sell advanced chips to China — and potentially even influenced President Trump’s own decisions surrounding AI export controls.

Jensen Huang would be a valuable target for a foreign adversary with sights on the American AI industry

US officials believe the Megaspeed executive is a foreign intelligence asset that has funneled information straight to the Chinese government, per The New York Times — in particular, officials reportedly believe that Megaspeed is related to a convoluted web of Chinese companies working together to access chips in bulk and perhaps even illegally get some of those chips into China. Alibaba is reportedly one of Megaspeed’s top customers.

“It’s not entirely surprising that the CEO of arguably one of the most important, if not the most important, AI chip companies is the target of some sort of intelligence-gathering from countries like China,” Hanna Dohmen, a senior research analyst at CSET, said in an interview with The Verge, adding that an alleged spy would potentially be interested in “better understanding what the US government is thinking on export controls,” as well as gathering information on Huang’s conversations with the Trump administration, attempting to influence policy, and gathering information on trade secrets like “who’s buying Nvidia’s chips, who’s getting them first, what’s coming next in terms of AI chips.”

Megaspeed’s sister company, headquartered in Malaysia, spent $4.8 billion or more on Nvidia chips and technology between June 2024 and February 2026, the Times reported, citing trade records from trade platform ImportGenius. The transaction sizes were outside the norm for a small company, particularly when Nvidia chips are so difficult to get.

”Meetings with customers are part of a CEO’s job”

Nvidia spokespeople had said Huang’s relationship with the Megaspeed executive was strictly business. Their interactions were described as “not unusual or unexpected” in statements to the press. Nvidia’s line was, “Meetings with customers are part of a CEO’s job.”

But at some point, their relationship became personal. In June 2024, just before Megaspeed became an Nvidia customer, photos show the two with other AI executives at a bar in Taipei after a local trade show; the following year, they reportedly had a business dinner in Taipei with others as well. But in private, according to US officials cited by the Times, the two’s relationship raised alarm bells for the US government — they had reportedly been surveilling the Megaspeed executive for months, if not longer, and that’s how it came out that she was in close contact with Huang.

The revelation is particularly concerning because of Huang’s lobbying role. He’d been trying to convince the Trump administration and Congress to loosen export controls for sending advanced semiconductors to China, ostensibly so that Nvidia could sell more chips. We now know this was happening around the same time that Huang was spotted at the Taiwan dinner with Alice Huang in May 2025, according to Culper Research, which shorted Nvidia’s stock earlier this year. That dinner occurred shortly after Nvidia had shared the Trump administration’s new restrictions on its China-specific H20 chips in April.

Just a couple months after the Taiwan dinner, Huang reportedly met with Trump in the Oval Office in July 2025 to plead his case for loosening export restrictions on Nvidia’s advanced semiconductors. Days later, the company announced that the administration had blessed sales of its H20 chips to China. Huang had argued that spreading American chips to China would help establish US technology as the standard, rather than allowing for Chinese chips to grow, according to The New York Times. After setbacks earlier in the second Trump term in export policy to China, Huang began speaking with then-White House AI czar David Sacks in 2025, who became the key advocate for Nvidia’s view that selling American chips to China would be beneficial, the Times reported.

By October 2025, Huang was lobbying Trump to allow Nvidia to sell more advanced chips to China, ahead of Trump’s meeting with Chinese President Xi Jinping, per the Times; but after Trump considered the proposal, he ultimately decided not to move forward. (That same month, Huang hired an external PR firm known for handling sex scandals, Wired reported.)

Months later, in December 2025, Trump changed course slightly, allowing Nvidia to sell H20 chips to a greenlit list of “approved customers” in China, with the US government taking a 25 percent cut of those sales. The same rules would apply to other US chipmakers, he wrote on Truth Social at the time.

“It is in Nvidia’s interest and in Jensen Huang’s interest to lobby for looser export control restrictions”

CSET’s Dohmen said that during the past two years, the US has seen a light loosening of AI export control regulations under the Trump administration, driven partly by Huang’s own lobbying. But it’s important to note, she said, that “even without any kind of intelligence operations from the Chinese side, it is in Nvidia’s interest and in Jensen Huang’s interest to lobby for looser export control restrictions.” Any restrictions by definition stifle Nvidia’s business expansion and cut off potential sales to help it grow its already stunning market cap — which is currently about $4.25 trillion, second only to Apple.

Huang’s relationship with Trump is also particularly relevant here. The president lavished praise on Huang during a speech last year, saying that until recently, he hadn’t even heard of Nvidia, and then he wanted to break it up. But after meeting Huang, he said, he understood why it would be difficult to re-create the company he’d built. More recently, Huang put Trump on speakerphone when the president called him during an appearance onstage at the All-In Summit, publicly displaying his close access to the Oval Office.

This past spring, a classified memo — the writing of which was overseen by Secretary of State Marco Rubio, per the Times — circulated among Trump administration officials ahead of the president’s trip to China in May, warning of the Megaspeed executive’s alleged involvement in surveillance on behalf of China’s Ministry of State Security. Her reported goal was to learn about advanced AI chips in the US and try to influence them being made available to China on a large scale. Asked if he had known about the memo reviewed by Rubio at a press briefing on Monday, Trump said, “I’d certainly check with the intelligence people. It could have been mentioned. Certainly it didn’t make much of an impact on me.” Earlier in the briefing, he said he was unaware of the alleged spy connection ahead of his trip to China.

Huang was initially left off the list of executives joining Trump on the trip, but the president later asked him to join. Trump had been briefed about a year ago that US intelligence believed the Megaspeed executive to be a China intelligence operative, according to the Times, and that she had a close relationship with a US citizen who turned out to be Nvidia’s CEO. At the time, he reportedly chose not to take action.

So far, the allegations haven’t affected Huang’s future at Nvidia. He’ll continue to lead the company during the investigation. Trump has also stood by him since news broke of the affair, telling reporters this past weekend, “I think he’s an honorable guy. I think he probably has an excuse for it. You have to hear it.”

Nvidia said it had “no reason to believe that either national security or Nvidia secrets were compromised”

On Sunday, Huang wrote an internal memo to Nvidia employees — some of which are his own family members — writing, “I owe my family and all of you an apology. I was unfaithful to my wife. My actions hurt her and our children. There is no excuse for what I did. I am deeply sorry.” He then addressed Nvidia’s board, partners, and shareholders, adding that he is “fully committed” to leading the company and “will work to earn back your confidence.” This weekend, Nvidia’s board of directors launched an independent investigation into the national security allegations. Huang will not have control over the participants in the investigation, and Nvidia said it had “no reason to believe that either national security or Nvidia secrets were compromised.”

Morningstar senior equity analyst Brian Colello wrote in a note on Monday that Morningstar “can’t rule out the investigation fading away and Nvidia returning to business as usual,” particularly since Huang is the “only CEO the company has ever known.” There’s also the fact that Huang’s Nvidia struck deals in August with six large financial institutions to provide more than $500 billion in financing for the buildout of AI data centers and other infrastructure, and as the US-China AI race intensifies, those are high-stakes agreements.

“It’s unclear to us what these partnerships and financing deals would look like with a different Nvidia CEO,” Colello wrote. “Costs of capital may rise for future investments if perhaps the most prominent CEO in the AI landscape is no longer orchestrating such deals.” Morningstar still maintained a very high uncertainty rating for the company, with Colello writing that it’s possible US approval of Nvidia to sell H20 chips to China will be revoked and that the company could ostensibly be sanctioned as well.

Trump told reporters on Sunday that Huang should remain CEO of Nvidia and that he would “certainly take him” on his next trip to China. “I haven’t heard he’s done anything wrong,” Trump told reporters. “He dealt with somebody, but you know, so does everybody else.”

articles.body:
President Trump held a White House press briefing earlier today and responded to several questions about his knowledge of Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang’s affair with an alleged Chinese spy. Huang said this weekend that he had been “unfaithful” to his wife, and the company has opened an investigation into Huang.

In a White House press conference, President Trump was vague about when learned of Jensen Huang’s affair.

Recent articles from The New York Times indicated that Trump had been aware of a relationship between Huang and Alice Huang, the suspected spy, before information about it became public. In October, The New York Times reported that Trump had been briefed “roughly a year ago” on intelligence that Huang and the alleged spy, Alice Huang, had developed a close relationship, but he didn’t do anything with the information. Yesterday, the NYT reported that Secretary of State Marco Rubio helped draft a memo to Trump officials about the relationship before Trump visited China in May.

In the press conference, Trump wasn’t specific about when he learned of the affair. But Trump said Huang told him today that he had “no idea” the person was a spy.

Here are Trump’s responses to questions about Jensen Huang from his press briefing today. You can watch a replay of the press conference on MS Now’s YouTube channel.

When were you first informed that there was an issue with Jensen Huang and the affair? What was presented to you at the time?

I would say that when I heard about it, first of all, I was amazed because I view him as a very high-quality person. I’ve known him a long time. It’s the largest, by value, the largest or one of the largest companies in the world. He did that with a chip. When you think about it, you’ve got a chip that’s 10 years advanced, can’t be… the Blackwell can’t even be copied. He’s an amazing guy.

I just hope there’s no problem. If there is a problem, we’ll let you know about it. But I hope there’s no problem. I believe he’s suffering greatly. I read his statement. And I believe he’s suffering greatly. Moreso because of his family. His wife who he loves and his family. But he is definitely suffering.

Just to follow up on the, “When were you first told of these potential issues with Mr. Huang?” You didn’t answer that question.

Well I’ve been hearing about it, and I’ve been reading a little bit about it over a period of time. But, not too long ago.

When is that?

We’ll look into it. I know the FBI’s looking into it in terms of something else. I think that he’ll be in good shape.

…

Are you going to bring up the case of Jensen Huang with President Xi when you visit with him next week?

No, I don’t think so. Maybe, I’m sure, President Xi will ask me about it. I just know Jensen very well. I just think he’s a very honorable man. He built a great company. American company. I think he’s a very honorable guy. I feel very confident that he’ll be in good shape.

Sticking with Jensen Huang, when you went to China earlier this year in May, did you know about these alleged ties to the spy then?

No, I didn’t hear about it then. But a lot of people have heard about it. And Jensen totally denies that. I asked him today, because I did speak to him today just to see if he’s feeling alright, how are you doing… and I asked him about that. He said he had absolutely no idea that the person in question was a spy. I asked him that question, did you have any idea that she was a spy? He said, I had no idea that she was a spy. And I really believe him.

…

I want to put a finer point on when exactly you were made aware of the intelligence around Jensen Huang.

Oh, I’d have to check. But this has been going on…

But there are reports that Secretary Rubio put an intelligence memo out last year. Did you read that memo?

I’d certainly check with the intelligence people. It could have been mentioned. Certainly it didn’t make much of an impact on me.

articles.body:
Six months before the Nvidia spy scandal emerged, the New York-based short seller firm Culper Research had already raised questions about Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang’s unusually close relationship with Alice Huang, an executive at Megaspeed, a Singapore-based company that buys Nvidia chips. She is now suspected to be a Chinese spy.

The Nvidia CEO admitted to an extramarital affair over the weekend, and the company has now opened a formal investigation into his relationship with Alice Huang (who shares his last name but is not related). U.S. intelligence officials believe she was recruited by the Chinese government to collect intelligence on Jensen Huang and influence his position regarding U.S. export controls on advanced AI chips.

Culper’s May 13 report is resurfacing because it picked up on the connection between Jensen Huang and Alice Huang while investigating Megaspeed’s ties to Nvidia.

In particular, the report called the relationship between the two executives “uncomfortably close,” noting that the Nvidia CEO was spotted partying and socializing with Alice Huang on multiple occasions. The report even claimed that some Nvidia employees wondered whether they had a “special relationship.”

Culper Research also theorized the China business that Nvidia lost to export controls had been rerouted through Southeast Asia, and that Megaspeed, a major chip buyer in the region, was secretly financed by Chinese tech giant Alibaba through shell companies. It pointed to financial records that showed Megaspeed’s total liabilities and equity had grown from $33 million at the end of 2023 to around $3 billion by the end of 2024, much of it in the form of refundable deposits from an unidentified source.

Financial Times reported Monday that documents show Alibaba lent money to Megaspeed through subsidiaries.

Culper is a short seller, so it stood to financially benefit from making these allegations, and those about possible illegal chip diversion have not been independently verified. Its report is available on the web and was posted to X back in May.

L'uomo al centro del caso di presunto spionaggio cinese è uno dei CEO più longevi e potenti del settore tecnologico

- Regala il Post

Quando un amministratore delegato finisce al centro di un presunto tentativo di spionaggio da parte di una potenza straniera, la sua posizione diventa molto difficile e le pressioni perché lasci l’incarico possono crescere rapidamente. Se poi quel CEO guidasse una delle aziende più strategiche nella competizione tecnologica internazionale, ci si aspetterebbe che anche le più alte cariche politiche del suo paese ne chiedessero le dimissioni. E la pressione sarebbe ancora maggiore se fosse anche uno dei consiglieri scelti direttamente dal presidente per orientare la politica del paese sulle tecnologie fondamentali per la sicurezza.

Nel caso di Jensen Huang, il CEO di Nvidia che ha ammesso di aver avuto una relazione con una donna sospettata di essere una spia assoldata dal governo cinese, sta succedendo quasi il contrario.

La donna in questione si chiama Alice Huang e, secondo quanto emerso da informazioni dell’intelligence statunitense riportate dalla stampa, potrebbe essere stata reclutata dalla Cina per raccogliere informazioni su Jensen Huang e su Nvidia. Il consiglio di amministrazione di Nvidia ha aperto un’indagine indipendente per capire se siano stati compromessi segreti aziendali o la sicurezza nazionale, ma allo stesso tempo ha ribadito pubblicamente di avere piena fiducia in lui. Il presidente degli Stati Uniti Donald Trump lo ha definito «una brava persona» e «un uomo onorevole», aggiungendo che probabilmente «ha una spiegazione» per quanto accaduto.

A spiegare tutta questa indulgenza è almeno in parte il ruolo che Huang ha dentro Nvidia, quotata come la seconda società al mondo e che finora nel 2026 ha generato 215,9 miliardi di dollari di ricavi, il 65 per cento in più rispetto all’anno precedente. Le sue GPU, chip progettati per eseguire moltissimi calcoli in parallelo, eseguono gran parte dei calcoli necessari per costruire e addestrare i modelli di intelligenza artificiale. Da loro dipendono aziende come OpenAI, Anthropic, Microsoft, Meta e Google.

Huang è uno dei CEO più longevi della Silicon Valley e non ha successori designati: una cosa che già all’inizio del 2026 Bloomberg aveva definito molto insolita per una società di tali dimensioni.

Huang è a capo di Nvidia da più di trent’anni: a lui vengono attribuite molte delle scelte decisive che l’hanno resa così grande ed è sempre lui a rappresentarla davanti a investitori, governi e clienti. Anche il suo modo di gestire l’azienda è diventato parte dell’identità di Nvidia: lui lo riassume provocatoriamente con l’espressione «torture them into greatness», più o meno «tormentali finché non diventano eccellenti»: dice di preferire continuare a mettere sotto pressione una persona perché migliori invece di rinunciarci e licenziarla.

Huang fondò Nvidia nel 1993 per costruire i chip che gestiscono la grafica dei videogiochi nei computer, insieme agli ingegneri Chris Malachowsky, ancora oggi dirigente tecnico dell’azienda, e Curtis Priem, che ne fu direttore tecnologico fino al 2003. Il loro primo prodotto portò Nvidia quasi al fallimento: il chip NV1, infatti, funzionava benissimo, ma elaborava la grafica tridimensionale con un sistema diverso da quello usato da Microsoft, che sarebbe poi diventato lo standard per la maggior parte degli sviluppatori.

Huang decise di cambiare approccio, licenziò metà dei dipendenti di Nvidia e scommise tutto su RIVA 128, un processore che non era nemmeno stato testato. Quando arrivò sul mercato, Nvidia aveva ormai denaro rimasto per circa un mese di stipendi. Ne vendette un milione di unità in quattro mesi: RIVA 128 offriva infatti in un’unica scheda grafica sia il 2D necessario per usare normalmente il computer, sia il 3D dei videogiochi, convincendo molti produttori di computer a installarlo direttamente nelle loro macchine.

Da quel momento, raccontano i suoi dipendenti, Huang ha cominciato a comportarsi come se il fallimento potesse essere sempre dietro l’angolo, una cosa che ha ricordato per anni nei suoi discorsi ai dipendenti.

In effetti i momenti difficili per Nvidia non erano finiti. Nel 2006 presentò CUDA, una piattaforma che permetteva di usare le GPU, che erano state sviluppate per la grafica dei videogiochi, anche per le simulazioni scientifiche e l’analisi di grandi quantità di dati. Huang decise di rendere tutte le sue GPU compatibili con CUDA, aumentando il costo dei chip al punto da assorbire i profitti lordi dell’azienda. Alla fine del 2008 il titolo Nvidia aveva perso circa il 70 per cento del suo valore.

Poi nel 2012 tre ricercatori mostrarono che quando una rete neurale, cioè il tipo di sistema alla base della maggior parte dell’intelligenza artificiale moderna, veniva addestrata utilizzando le GPU di Nvidia poteva ottenere risultati eccezionali nel riconoscimento delle immagini. Huang decise così di investire tutto nell’intelligenza artificiale: un dirigente dell’azienda, Greg Estes, ha raccontato che Huang comunicò la decisione con una mail inviata un venerdì sera e che il lunedì Nvidia si comportava già come un’azienda di AI.

Huang fece una scommessa simile anche con i data center quando nel 2019 decise di investire 6,9 miliardi di dollari per Mellanox, un’azienda specializzata nelle tecnologie che permettono a migliaia di processori di comunicare ad altissima velocità. Era la tecnologia che poi sarebbe stata alla base del funzionamento delle IA, che richiedono migliaia o decine di migliaia di GPU collegate tra loro.

Tutto questo è stato possibile anche per il modo in cui Huang gestisce l’azienda: ci sono circa sessanta dirigenti e Huang ha incontri diretti con tutti loro. Organizza le riunioni in modo che le discussioni avvengano davanti a più persone contemporaneamente, per far sì che tutti possano ascoltare quale sia il problema, il ragionamento con cui viene affrontato e il percorso che porta alla soluzione. Anche gli errori vengono trattati allo stesso modo: Huang chiede ai suoi dipendenti di presentare davanti a centinaia di persone la catena di decisioni che hanno portato a un errore, in modo che tutti possano evitare di ripeterla.

Huang ha anche reso Nvidia un’azienda di famiglia, una cosa insolita nella Silicon Valley. Ci lavorano il figlio Spencer Huang, la figlia Madison Huang e il genero. La moglie Lori Huang, invece, presiede la Jen-Hsun & Lori Huang Foundation, un ente che finanzia università, ricerca e progetti filantropici. La vicenda, che ha fatto emergere le vulnerabilità della sicurezza aziendale, rischia di avere ripercussioni anche sugli equilibri interni e sulla gestione di Nvidia, coinvolgendo direttamente una famiglia diventata negli ultimi anni sempre più presente e visibile nell’azienda. Huang aveva persino detto, quando i figli erano più giovani, che il suo sogno sarebbe stato vedere un giorno uno di loro guidare Nvidia.

Quando in un’intervista venne detto a Huang che i suoi collaboratori lo descrivevano come «esigente», «perfezionista» e una persona «non facile per cui lavorare», lui rispose che la descrizione era perfettamente corretta e che fare cose straordinarie non è facile.

FederUnacoma: l’aumento dei costi produttivi impatta anche sul mercato dei trattori. calo del 5,4% in Italia e del 13% negli Usa. La presidente Maschio: le vendite ripartiranno

L’esplosione dei costi produttivi sta provocando una profonda erosione dei redditi agricoli. E con la flessione dei redditi mancano i presupposti per favorire gli investimenti in macchine e tecnologie per l’agricoltura. È con questo complesso scenario congiunturale che si apre oggi a Bologna l’edizione 2026 di Eima, il salone delle macchine e delle tecnologie per l’agricoltura organizzato da FederUnacoma (l’associazione dei costruttori italiani).

Forte calo dei redditi in Europa e Usa

«I produttori agricoli – ha spiegato la presidente di FederUnacoma, Mariateresa Maschio ricevono una quota molto limitata del prezzo che i consumatori pagano. Negli Stati Uniti, le aziende ricevono meno di 12 centesimi di ogni dollaro di cibo prodotto, quota che cala a 6,7 cent al netto dei costi. In Europa i produttori ottengono circa un quarto del valore aggiunto della filiera agroalimentare. Una quota che rischia di ridursi ancora a causa dell’incremento dei costi».

E con i redditi frenano anche gli investimenti

Difficoltà che si riversano sul mercato dei macchinari. I dati aggiornati ad ottobre - elaborati da FederUnacoma sulla base delle immatricolazioni fornite dal Ministero dei Trasporti - indicano un calo del 5,4% per le trattrici, del 9% per i trasponder, del 7,3% per i rimorchi. Restano in positivo solo le mietitrebbiatrici (+10,4% a fronte di 245 macchine vendute).

Cala il mercato nazionale ma anche quello internazionale. Negli Stati Uniti, tra gennaio e settembre le trattrici hanno perso il 13%. In Canada le vendite hanno registrato un -9%. Peggio ancora in America Latina con la flessione del 19% in Brasile e del -27% in Argentina. Meno accentuate ma sempre in negativo le vendite in Europa il -6% della Germania, il -3,3% della Francia, il -4,6% della Spagna e il -18,8% della Polonia.

Un ridimensionamento del mercato che spinge alla frenata la produzione nazionale che, secondo le stime di FederUnacoma, dovrebbe vedere nel 2026 un calo in valore della produzione di trattrici del 4,7% (a quota 1,8 miliardi di euro).

articles.body:
L’analisi congiunturale di Bankitalia registra un Pil a 0,9%, come quello italiano. Nei porti liguri calano (di poco) traffici, container e passeggeri

Nella prima parte del 2026 l’attività economica in Liguria ha continuato a crescere moderatamente; secondo l’indicatore trimestrale dell’economia regionale (Iter) elaborato dalla Banca d’Italia, nel primo semestre il prodotto interno lordo sarebbe aumentato dello 0,9% (come in Italia). E in base al consueto sondaggio condotto da Bankitalia sul tessuto imprenditoriale, nei primi tre trimestri dell’anno, nell’industria in senso stretto, sono aumentati sia la produzione sia il fatturato; le aspettative a breve termine, inoltre, sono cautamente ottimistiche, sebbene, rileva il report, «esposte a rischi al ribasso».

Nel primo semestre, rileva Bankitalia, le esportazioni a prezzi correnti sono cresciute (+8,3%), anche al netto delle componenti più volatili. L’attività edilizia si è stabilizzata: il numero delle ore lavorate segnalate alle Casse edili è rimasto invariato (+0,1%). Il comparto edilizio, infatti, ha continuato a trarre vantaggio dall’avanzamento dei lavori relativi alle principali opere pubbliche. Nel settore immobiliare, sono aumentate le transazioni sia nel segmento abitativo sia in quello non residenziale (rispettivamente +4,9 e +4,5%).

Secondo il sondaggio, nel complesso, il fatturato delle imprese del terziario è cresciuto. Tra gennaio e settembre le presenze turistiche sono aumentate (+1,8%), sospinte soprattutto dalla componente italiana (+2,6). Nel primo semestre dell’anno, il numero dei passeggeri in transito nei porti regionali si è ridotto (-1,5%), per effetto del calo dei fruitori dei traghetti. Il traffico commerciale marittimo è diminuito leggermente (-1,3%); anche il numero dei container movimentati è sceso (-0,9%).

La situazione economico finanziaria delle imprese, sottolinea il report, «è rimasta favorevole: la maggior parte delle aziende liguri (l’87%) prevede di conseguire un utile nel 2026; la liquidità è aumentata, avvicinandosi ai massimi del 2023. Nel complesso, i finanziamenti al comparto produttivo si sono ridotti (-3,7%), anche per effetto delle scelte di indebitamento di alcuni grossi operatori».

Nonostante la ripresa dell’inflazione, «alimentata anche dalle tensioni in Medioriente, la positiva situazione del mercato del lavoro ha sostenuto il reddito delle famiglie, il cui andamento ha favorito un moderato incremento dei consumi in termini reali (+1,2%). Nell’ambito del risparmio finanziario, i depositi delle famiglie e delle imprese liguri sono tornati nel complesso ad aumentare (+1,5%).

articles.body:
EU seeks to pick new ECB head by year end: Eurogroup chief said

November 9, 2026

Christine Lagarde's decision to step down early as head of the European Central Bank (ECB) has put the European Union on a tight schedule. The bloc expects to pick a new ECB chief by the end of December.

The European Union (EU) wants to name the next head of the European Central Bank by the end of the year, Eurogroup chief Kyriakos Pierrakakis said Monday.

Christine Lagarde, who has headed the ECB for seven years, announced on October 29 that she is stepping down from the position prematurely, nine months before the end of her term.

Lagarde's decision to step down early makes the schedule tight for EU leaders because they must also fill two other seats on the ECB's Executive Board within months.

"The ambition here is that the whole process would have completed itself by the end of the year," Pierrakakis said before a Eurogroup meeting of eurozone finance ministers.

"We understand that we need to move fast. But what has traditionally happened in the past is that this was a decision driven by the leaders. Today it will be primarily an information point and the discussion," he said.

Who are the candidates?

The two candidates to replace Lagarde are former Dutch Central Bank Governor Klaas Knot and the head of the Bank for International Settlements, Pablo Hernandez de Cos from Spain.

Pierrakakis said that Dutch and Spanish ministers would present their candidates and that later on Monday he would meet with Antonio Costa, head of the European Council, which represents EU governments' heads.

The appointment process requires eurozone finance ministers to put forward a candidate, followed by a European Parliament hearing and a final decision by EU leaders.

Dutch minister says the choice needs to be 'merit based'

Spanish Economy Minister Carlos Cuerpo said Hernandez de Cos was the "right person for the position," referring to his long-standing experience.

"He knows the ECB inside out. He's been leading institutions such as the Bank of Spain, such as BIS as well. A steady hand, but always a profile to be able to find consensus," he told reporters.

Dutch Finance Minister Eelco Heinen, on the other hand, said Knot was an "excellent candidate", adding: "He has a very clear understanding of the ECB mandate and he has... a lot of experience to fulfill this position."

Heinen also said countries should not see the ECB leadership contest as one between northern and southern European countries, or as an "opportunity to trade favors" on other topics such as the multi-year EU budget.

A package deal is expected

The other two seats which have to be filled are those of Isabel Schnabel, the head of the ECB's market operations, who leaves on January 3, 2027, and Chief Economist Philip Lane, whose term ends in May 2027.

The three jobs are likely to be negotiated between the main eurozone countries — France, Germany, Spain and the Netherlands — as a package, Reuters news agency said, citing officials.

The expectation is that the leaders agree on a package deal on all three positions.

"Perhaps this would facilitate things. But again, this is a decision that will be taken by the leaders at the leaders level," Pierrakakis said.

Irish Finance Minister Simon Harris, whose country holds the rotating EU presidency, said he hoped Lagarde's replacement would be chosen by December.

"It certainly makes sense to fill the vacancy as quickly as possible," he said. But it's also about getting it right and getting the right person. It's a really crucial appointment."
